That is why I make this appeal to the government. Do not say this is merely a clarification, because then the men on the line will say "If that is so, we cannot get any more." It is the right of the railway workers to negotiate for something over the 18 per cent which they have already rejected and against which they went out on strike. Therefore, if the union nominee did not sign it and the unions did not accept it, this means they struck against the particular recommendation that was made.
I listened yesterday to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration with admiration

DEBATES	September 1, 1966
and sadness; admiration for his great eloquence and passion, sadness that they were used to make an elaborate and agonizing rationalization for a position that must have been untenable to him. Each one of us feels he has to do the things he believes himself impelled to do. If that is what the minister wanted to do it is, of course, his right. During the course of his speech, in reply to an interjection of mine, he said there are two kinds of commitments, one a legal guarantee and the other a moral guarantee, and he waxed eloquent about the second.
There was once a labour leader in this country, a man now dead, whose name was Silby Barrett. He was a miner with a definite, characteristic way of speaking. He used to tell us that when he was engaged in negotiations and the employer said to him "You don't have to write everything down, we can have a gentleman's agreement," his reply- and I am using his rather picturesque language-was, "Every time an employer says that to me, I says to him a verbal agreement ain't worth the paper it's writ on."
Lest anyone think Mr. Silby Barrett was wrong I remind the committee that the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration talked a great deal about precedents. Let me draw to his attention a precedent recorded in Hansard. In 1950 there was a railway strike, and among the union groups involved were hotel employees and water transport employees and their organizations. During the time the bill to end that strike was before this house in 1950 the C.C.F, members at that time, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, the late member for Vancouver East at that time, and Mr. M. J. Coldwell, drew to the attention of the prime minister of the day, Mr. St. Laurent, that a section of that act was ambiguous and ran the danger of leaving the hotel employees and the water transport employees out on a limb, and that they would not be treated in the same way.
[DOT] (11:10 a.m.)
In answer to these charges raised by members of the C.C.F., Mr. St. Laurent, the then prime minister, at page 75 of Hansard for August 30, 1950 said:
They-
Referring to the hotel employees and the water transport employees.
-are not being discriminated against in any way. The government, in the bill which it recommended to parliament, has treated them in the same way as the other unions, namely, as one unit; and everything that binds the arbitrator
September 1, 1966

with respect to any one binds him as much with respect to those two small groups as it does to the others.
Later on in his remarks he said:

Then the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre interjected and said:
Let us have this clear. The Prime Minister Just said that the arbitrator is bound in his dealings with the hotel and water transport workers in the same way as in his dealings with the others.
He said something more and in answer to that Mr. St. Laurent said that he would not like to discuss those details. The hon. member had referred to some details. Mr. St. Laurent continued:
.. . but in the recomendation we made to parliament and in the bill itself we have attempted to treat as one unit all those involved in this *dispute. On all of the points in which we have provided expressly, we have stated the arbitrator cannot undo what we are doing.
The unions came before the arbitrator, Mr. Justice Kellock. At the very beginning of the discussion the leader of the railway unions, Mr. Hall, drew his attention to the statements of the prime minister. Mr. Justice Kellock in connection with the principles of the interpretation of statutes said:
The principle is that you get what parliament Intended from the statute, that the statute is the collective decision. You do not take what some individual said in discussion.
As a result, when the award was brought down by the arbitrator the hotel employees and water transport employees received a smaller wage increase; their contract was for a different term, and they did not get the 40 hour week which the railway workers got. That is your moral guarantee, made at that time in all good faith, I am certain, and with the utmost sincerity, I am certain, by the prime minister of that day. When you interpret a statute the only kind of guarantee is to have it in the statute. That is the reason I am glad the government has accepted the representations made not only in this house but made to the Prime Minister and perhaps to the Minister of Labour by the leaders of the railway unions involved.

I demonstrated to the minister that they are not in all cases adequate, and that when you
DEBATES	7945
Legislation Respecting Railway Matters are dealing with a piece of legislation which is going to come before a tribunal which is going to have to interpret it, it is not only inadequate but is irrelevant. The arbitrator may say that he is not bound by what the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration says. He may say that the minister is a very fine gentleman but that the principles of interpretations of a statute are that the statute speaks for itself. Therefore it is of the utmost importance that it be in the bill. If it is not in the bill it is of no effect at all, and the most flowery and eloquent words of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration-and there were many of them-cannot possibly persuade any arbitrator that that is what the law is when in fact it does not say it.
Another reason I welcome the amendment is that it now can become, and I hope it will, the floor rather than the ceiling, and that the unions will be able to negotiate-and I hope they will succeed in the negotiation-something above that. Last night the Minister of Labour quoted from a conciliation board report which I had signed to the effect that I supported the durable goods standard. The other day I indicated that in my opinion the only way to avoid the possibility of strikes in the railway industry is to set up an objective standard by which the terms and conditions of work for railway employees are measured. We must have an outside comparison and that comparison must be-as I have said on many occasions and in a number of reports which I either wrote myself or which the chairman wrote and I signed-one which makes it clear that the employees of the railways are not subsidizing public policy. As I indicated the other day in respect of the new Railway Act it will be inevitable for decades to come that the railways will be required to carry certain freight at rates less than they might otherwise charge and will be required to carry on passenger services which in their view are uneconomic.
We will require that because Canada requires it. It is right that they should do so. But so long as we require it, so long also will it be necessary for all the people of Canada to make it possible for the railways to carry freight at less than the charge they would otherwise make. There is nothing wrong with the public treasury making that possible. That is the only way we can have a transportation system in Canada. We cannot run it any other way. Therefore over the years that I have been a member of railway conciliation boards, we have taken the position, which I
7946	COMMONS
Legislation Respecting Railway Matters think is a correct one, that you must have an outside standard of comparison, one which gives the railway workers an adequate return and decent conditions so they are not required to subsidize the decisions of public policy for Canada as a whole.
The durable goods standard was chosen. I hope members of the committee may forgive me if I put some of this history on the record. The durable goods standard was chosen, in the words of Mr. Justice Kellock in 1952, because it was comparable, he said, "as nearly as may be". At that time the comparison was between the average of the hourly earnings of all the non-op employees and the average of the earnings of all employees in the durable goods industry. This was in 1952.
As I suggested the other night, only in one year since 1952 have the railway employees been in a parallel position to that of the durable goods standard, namely in 1953. You will find this in the report of the union nominee, Mr. Crowe. Every year since then they have been paid between 4 per cent and 5 per cent below the durable goods earnings. The research worker for the railway unions informed the board of conciliation that according to his calculations this 4 per cent to 5 per cent below the standard, which they were told they ought to be able to enjoy, was equivalent for each of the 120,000 employees involved to $2,700 over the period.
Why were they below the durable goods standard? This also is of interest and it will take me only a minute or two to put it to the committee.
[DOT] (11:20 a.m.)
In 1954 the railway unions, looking at the situation in Canada-and this is the trademark of railway employees to some extent-found that the railway workers, except for a pension plan which was as good as most pension plans in the country, had none or almost none of the other fringe benefits. They had no statutory holidays in their contract, no medical plan and no sick leave provision. They decided in 1954 that they would ask for some of these fringe benefits. Being responsible unions-and some of their members have said to me that they are a little too responsible about this kind of thing-they decided to ask for fringe benefits only and not a wage increase, because the fringe benefits were going to be costly if they were to be granted. The result was that between 1952 and 1956, for

DEBATES	September 1, 1966
four years, the railway workers did not receive a single penny by way of a wage increase. That put them below the durable goods standard to a substantial extent.
When the board of which I was a member looked at the situation in 1956 the chairman decided-and I must say that rather reluctantly but in logic I had to agree with him-it was impossible in one fell swoop to wipe out the entire gap and an award was made that still kept them below the durable goods standard, and this situation was perpetuated.
What in effect has happened is that the railway workers and their unions have said in 1966, with the economy going full blast, with the railways' earnings at the highest level in their history making considerable, indeed, huge profits, this is the year they must catch up and get themselves in a position of real comparison with their likes in outside industries. In order to make the durable goods standard not only comparable "as nearly as it may be", but more comparable so that the comparison is really like with like, the unions proposed, and to me it is thoroughly logical, that the durable goods earnings be adjusted in respect of certain differences between the mix of the durable work force and the mix of the non-operating work force. This would justify a further increase in my opinion of 25 per cent. Thus I say to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration that in proposing a 25 per cent increase the other day-I was not bargaining-I did so because it seemed to me that what Mr. Crowe recommended, on the basis of the evidence of the unions, was entirely logical and right.
I could spend a good deal of time insisting, as the right hon. Leader of the Opposition has done, that the government caved in or gave in, and I agree with that position; but I suggest to him and to all other members of the house there is nothing I could add that would give the point more emphasis. What is important at this time-and I appeal to the government with all the seriousness I can command to believe that what I say is valid, now that this amendment has been made-is to make sure it is acceptable to the workers. In addition to the Freedman report and the other things that have been mentioned, the thing that will make it acceptable to them is a clear admission by the government and a recognition by parliament, by the news media and by the people of Canada, that what the law now provides is that the railway unions have a right to come before a mediator or arbitrator to seek a 25 per cent increase or an
September 1, 1966	COMMONS
increase anywhere between 18 and 25 per cent.
I appeal to the government not to insist that the purpose of this amendment is a mere clarification. It is not just that; it is a fundamental change in the principle of the bill.

Mr. Chairman, I want to make a few remarks on my own behalf and on behalf of my party, on the amendment to clause 6 which we hoped for whole-heartedly.
I shall not take too much of the time of the house, because too many speakers have done so since last Monday. I believe that if Canada's population had seen certain shows in this chamber, it would be very sorry for the behaviour of this house in such a case. It seems to me that the situation in Canada is too serious to engage in politicking, to play with words and to try and get out of a bill a meaning that is not in it and to try and gain popularity to the prejudice of labour and industry and of all those who call us on the telephone all day long to ask us to bring this strike to its conclusion.
[DOT] (11:40 a.m.)
Mr. Chairman, as far as our party is concerned, we have done all we could; only two of our members spoke and they simply expressed our general views on this strike and on what we expected of the government.
Mr. Chairman, the hon. Minister of Manpower (Mr. Marchand) told us that the question of wages and working conditions could not be wholly dealt with by this house. According to what we have heard in this house these last few days, I agree with the minister one hundred per cent that if a collective agreement had to be drawn up, it would take at least, two years, especially in the atmosphere now prevailing in this house.
I think that if political games could be stopped on both sides, discussions would be a lot more simple. But, unfortunately, you cannot prevent a politician from playing politics
7950	COMMONS
Legislation Respecting Railway Matters any more than a doctor from practising medicine.
One thing we can prevent, however, is excesses. And heavens knows that we have had our fill of excesses since Monday, Mr. Chairman; I hope the house will show some sense of responsibility so that the bill will be passed by this evening.
However, things would have been much simpler if the government had introduced clear legislation instead of getting lost in implications, clause 6 is a striking example. In fact, if the government had inserted in the bill right from the start what it was finally compelled to put in by way of amendment, the Minister of Manpower would not have been exposed to ridicule following the famous speech he made to try to make us see some moral sense in Bill No. C-230.
We understood his remarks to mean that he wanted to leave the final decision to those who are truly responsible and that was not so bad but it is even better when the legislation spells out that the immediate increase will be the basis of future negotiations and not a moral ceiling, as stated in the original bill and as claimed by some hon. members. It is mostly that point which caused 75 per cent of the misunderstanding and useless discussions.
Under the amendment, railway workers will then get an increase of 4 per cent retroactive to January 1966, another one of 4 per cent retroactive to July 1966, a third one of 4 per cent in January 1967 and an additional one of 6 per cent in July 1967. Contrary to what the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) and others who seek to reap a political advantage from this, the amendment was not moved at the suggestion of the opposition; it was just simply proposed by the various boards.
That is why I stated at the beginning of my remarks that the debate could have taken only one day if the bill had been drawn along the lines of the board recommendations. It will remain for the mediators and the two parties concerned to make the final adjustments. If those terms had been as clear as they are now, we would already be considering the second bill.
But something else has me puzzled, since I met the members of the Canadian Brotherhood of Railway and Transport Workers which has 23,000 members. It is a wholly Canadian union but affiliated to the American Railway Workers Unions. That group is completely opposed to increases on the present

DEBATES	September 1. 1966
percentage basis, because once again that favours the highly-paid people.
Mr. Chairman, I have here the brief submitted by the Canadian Brotherhood which reads in part as follows:
The requests made by the Brotherhood are as follows
that all wage rates be increased by 90 cents per hour-
-that an employee with at least two years of service must not be laid off, etc.
The brief deals with working conditions, but our concern as regards clause 6 of Bill No. C-230 is the financial terms; therefore, I will not wander from the subject, like the Leader of the Opposition did so well last night. I will keep to the salary conditions. And to prove it, Mr. Chairman, the said 18 per cent which those who really need it, that is the small wage-earners, will get is equivalent to 20, 25 or 30 cents per hour, whereas the highly-paid people will get $1, $1.10 and $1.15 more.
I submit that it is precisely about that class of workers that we should think. To get a concrete example, I questioned a few workers. For instance, a clerk with a family, who has been working for the C.N.R. for 20 years, today earns $360 a month, for 174 hours of work, that is $2.05 per hour.
Another employee, who looks after the maintenance of a passenger train, earns $1.90 per hour after 15 years. An engineer earns $2.25 per hour after 40 years, and should he have an unfortunate accident like the one I mentioned last winter in my region, because he has to work under inadmissible conditions, the authorities of the C.N.R. hasten to give him a ticket. Another operating employee with 25 years experience earns $170 per week. It is a good salary, but he works 96 hours a week, which means $2.10 per hour. I would like to give you a host of cases in those classes of workers where clearly ridiculous salaries are paid, without talking about the conditions in which they have to live.
If you study the situation seriously, for some of them, the salaries are not adequate and for others, working conditions are not what they should be. On the matter of salaries, I prefer the proposal made by the Canadian Brotherhood of Railway Employees, namely an increase of 90 cents per hour instead of 18, 20 and even 30 per cent. I will go even further, Mr. Chairman, and say that to be fair and to give a equitable increase, that increase should be limited to wages of
September 1, 1966

$12,000 or less, in short, no increase should be allowed to those earning $12,000 or more, but 90 cents an hour should be given to those earning $12,000 or less. I think the proposal would be a great deal fairer.
Would the Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson) tell us whether that brief has been discussed during meetings with unions. It appears to have been ignored completely, since not a word has been heard about it since Monday. Were the voices of those trade-unionists who are, after all, 20,000 in number, neutralized under the power of American unions? I would like to know the views of the Minister of Labour in that respect.
As far as the requests of the Brotherhood are concerned, I trust their voices will be heard in committee and that the next mediator will allow the small ones as well as the big ones to have a say in the matter. We are, therefore, expecting the report which, according to the bill, will be submitted to us on November 15,	1966, to put forth proper
claims.
[DOT] (11:50 a.m.)
In the meantime, everyone should assume his responsibilities because Mr. Chairman, I am afraid that in that whole matter parliament is not alone responsible for this state of affairs.
If we consider the Canadian National authorities, the chairman, the directors, who are 11 in number, the administrators who are 23 or 24 in number, we wonder whether they are not responsible for the disaster. That is why I also ask the Minister of Labour, the cabinet which appoints those persons, which is responsible for them, to try to find out whether they treated the workers as they should have, whether they did not instead remain undisturbed in their ivory tower and left the workers struggle with their poor wages and abject working conditions.
I think the culminating point of all that matter is to be found more with management than with the workers. We now have a group of administrators who seem to consider only the fabulous salary. When we consider, for example, $75,000 a year, apart from expenses, which amount to about $100,000 for the president of the Canadian National, will someone tell me that the chairman of the Canadian National is greater, more competent, has more responsibilities than the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson)? And yet he is paid twice as much as the Prime Minister! Well, this is a democracy-I am told he is more competent-and I have to consider the position to
7951
Legislation Respecting Railway Matters which he was elected by the people, but, I think that if Mr. Donald Gordon were running in an election, he would not receive 250 votes. When we compare the salary of that man with that of the leader of Canada, I say that not one civil servant should draw more than the leader of Canada. And here, Mr. Chairman, I want to call the attention of the cabinet to the fact that that race for salaries must come to an end. Is there some collusion between them, because not a word is heard, not one blame is made, and that in any crown corporation. Take the C.B.C. it is the same thing. They raise their own salaries. At the end of the year, they have a deficit. When they have a deficit, when they are in trouble, as we have just had with the workers, then they come to us and say: Sirs, you are the friends of the people, come and protect us, come and pay the deficit, go before the union members and help settle our mistakes, while we continue to take it easy.
Mr. Chairman, I call the attention of the Minister of Labour, of the cabinet, of the whole cabinet and of parliament to these blood-suckers who are mocking us, mocking parliament with their catastrophic salaries and who help put crown corporations in the red. And we accept that. Yes, we accept that. No, Mr. Chairman, I say that this state of affairs must cease and that all should assume their responsibilities. If the responsibility for the current strike lies with the authorities, let them be judged and if they have to be fired, let them be fired. That is all. For there is not a man better prepared than the president and the directors responsible for C.N.R. transport more qualified to deal with the worker. He is in a position to know what he needs, to know the conditions, and to set him up in a humane position, in a social environment where the worker will enjoy life.
That is the duty of those who have been appointed by the government and who are responsible for the Canadian National. It may be nice to hold a job, to have all the salary and refuse all responsibilities. Mr. Chairman, I say it is the responsibility of the cabinet to look into this and force those in charge of crown corporations to settle the working conditions of labour, the working conditions of crown employees, and if they cannot agree, let us throw them out.
Throw them out. Period. Being uninformed about the detailed organization of these companies, members of the house are unable to form an opinion. That is why, as I said earlier, the Minister of Manpower (Mr. Marchand) was right in saying that it was not
7952	COMMONS
Legislation Respecting Railway Matters up to the members of the house to deal with collective bargaining because they were not qualified to do so. It belongs to those people. Let everyone exercise his rights, carry out his own duties and mind his own business.
I ask the Minister of Labour to consider this aspect of the problem during the committee stage and stop bearing down the members right and left. Some people claim that we are not settling the strike. But really, how can we go about settling a strike? What is the use of a disagreement between employers and workers? What business is it of ours, logically? If every man assumed his responsibilities, if C.N.R. authorities assumed their responsibilities, there would not be any strike, because, after all, we are politicians and in studying this matter, we realize it is simply ridiculous to linger over the question of salaries of the railway workers, because we pay a salary to those who remain idle and allow the workers to starve, those who operate the railways.
In addition, those people are constantly badgered by five or six inspectors and auditors. I note that top management comprises approximately one third of the employees. They are greenhorns, just out of university who come to inspect. I saw in my area three inspectors conduct a little investigation during a week at the railway station-I shall not give any name because they will get after them-and where the agent could have done much better than they did at no cost at all. But I would not have liked to pay the bill of those three puppies who strutted around town for a week.
There must be an end to this with regard to the C.N.R. I saw two employees working on the tracks and three "foremen" supervising their work. Well, now.-

I therefore hope that the hon. minister will seriously consider what I have just said.

Mr. Chairman, last night when the Minister of Labour announced his intention to move an amendment to clause 6 when it was reached, and then read the words of the amendment he intended to move, I suggested there were some defects in the wording if it were meant to give effect to what the Minister of Labour, the Minister of National Health and Welfare, the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration and the Prime Minister were saying would be the intent of the amendment. As I read the amendment today I see there are still two serious defects in the legal terms which are required by statutes in order to achieve what I think the government and I am sure all members of the house hope will be the effect of the amendment.
In the first instance, I think the purpose of amending clause 6 is to provide a 4 per cent increase effective January 1, 1967 and an additional 6 per cent on July 1, 1967, not to amend the collective agreements which expired at the end of December, 1965. The clause put forward the minimum figure for arbitration purposes if arbitration becomes necessary.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I do not think it is right or proper to suggest that the intention is to amend clause 6 so as to change the collective agreements by statute and fix that percentage as the amount of the increase. Surely if we are to take seriously the statements which have been made by ministers both yesterday and today-and I hope I can take them seriously-this is to be a minimum figure, not a fixed amount.
There is one other serious defect in the wording of the amendment, and it is this. While it speaks of an additional 4 per cent effective January 1, 1967 and another 6 per
September 1, 1966

cent on July 1, 1967, I suggest it is possible, in view of the present wording of the clause, that some individual employees may not receive an 18 per cent increase. I suggest it is possible that the mediator or arbitration board could interpret the wording as setting an average increase of 18 per cent. Some employees might only receive 14 per cent or 12 per cent while others might receive over 18 per cent, but it would average out to 18 per cent. Since in my view that result is possible-and I have consulted some competent people in this matter-I think this would be a breach of faith so far as the workers are concerned and a violation of what is intended.
There has been far too much misrepresentation, if you want to call it that, or at least misunderstanding, up to this point of the debate about what parliament intends to do in connection with this dispute. Surely, Mr. Chairman, having now reached the stage where it seems that all parties agree that the intent of the amendment is good, we should use language which will avoid any breach of faith when the final arbitration decision is handed down, if things go that far.
I know there are differences in the amounts which should be granted to various categories or classes of employees. I think there are some who in justice should have relatively larger increases than others. But I suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, to the government and particularly to the Minister of Labour that there is room above the 18 per cent minimum figure to make these adjustments. I do not think this parliament should now, after we have had all this difficulty, approve an amendment which will in fact legally allow an average increase of 18 per cent rather than provide an increase of 18 per cent as a guaranteed minimum to every single employee coming within the two categories under the collective agreements which are discussed in clause 6.
After the indication was given last night that this amendment would be introduced I telephoned a number of representatives of the labour unions and told them 1 thought they could tell their members that each one of them, if they went back to work, could expect to receive nothing less than at least an 18 per cent increase. They replied that if other considerations were referred to the mediator or arbitration board, relating to other fringe benefits, the question of job security and so on, they were of the opinion that the employees would probably accept
7953
Legislation Respecting Railway Matters them, would obey an order of parliament and would go back to work.
I think if we ask them to do that the language which is used should make it so abundantly clear that there can be no misinterpretation and none of them will find themselves three or four months from now with an increase of something less than 18 per cent; that this figure of 18 per cent was meant to be a minimum and that some employees would receive more than that figure. It would be disastrous for parliament to leave the impression that we are passing a law to guarantee this minimum if it does not turn out that way. As I said before, there is room above the 18 per cent for those categories of employees needing special consideration.
[DOT] (12:10 p.m.)
I implore the Minister of Labour to do something about this situation. I have looked at his amendment and considered various means of moving a subamendment which would correct it to give effect to the proposal I have been making. It would take some time to do this because I think the proposal should be spelled out in detail so the mediator or arbitration board would be bound by it.
What I ask now is that the minister withdraw this amendment. This is the simplest way of handling the difficulty. If he wishes, he can have my amendment and move it himself. I do not care whether I move it or not. I believe it spells out what is intended. To support this contention I could quote from the speech made last evening by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration. I will quote a paragraph from the report which appeared in today's Gazette:
At one point, Mr. Marchand declared that If he were not convinced, utterly convinced, that the strikers could be certain of a wage increase interim settlement of "at least" 18 per cent, "I would oppose the bill."
Surely this means 18 per cent for each individual worker. The report of the minister's statement continues:
There was, he said, a "moral guarantee" to the railwaymen that nothing less would be available.
Then the Prime Minister himself is quoted as giving a similar assurance. In other words there is no thought that the total increase over the two year period will be any less than 18 per cent reached in four instalments, as recommended by Mr. Justice Munroe and Mr. Justice Cameron. I believe this is what is intended, and this is what the legislation should make clear. I do not have a copy of
7954	COMMONS
Legislation Respecting Railway Matters Hansard for yesterday-copies may be available now, but I could not get one a few minutes ago-but in today's issue of the Globe and Mail I see the following:
The Prime Minister told the commons that the government bill ordering an end to the strike had always been intended to ensure the minimum 18 per cent pay boost recommended by two conciliation boards.
Surely this means that the increase applies to every single employee and that the figure is not to be an average of 18 per cent so that some employees would find themselves given less. On this point I could quote further from the speeches by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration and the Minister of National Health and Welfare. It seems abundantly clear that every employee can expect a minimum of 18 per cent, but this is now what could be the effect of the amendment. I should like the minister to give this house a firm assurance that this amendment will guarantee every single employee a minimum of 18 per cent; or does he say it is only an average that we are talking about?
Again I ask the minister to do the simplest thing; to withdraw this amendment and bring in another which does meet the point I have raised. The amendment I have prepared says:
That the terms and conditions of any amendment or revision of the collective agreements to which this act applies, determined under the provisions of sections 8, 9 or 10 of this act, shall provide at least an increase of not less than 4 per cent and not less than an additional 6 per cent for the two respective dates in 1967.
We have had enough confusion, enough delay, misinterpretation and misunderstanding. Let us not now make any mistake concerning the terms which are binding on the arbitration board as a result of the instructions in this legislation. I ask the minister to make the changes for which I have been arguing.

I wish to thank the hon. member for Medicine Hat not only for his remarks this morning but for his contribution to the debate last night and for the material with which he supplied me. What disturbs me about the suggestion put forward by the hon. gentleman is this. We now have a formula produced by Judge Munroe and concurred in by Hon. Mr. Cameron, that is, 4-4-4-6. No one would disagree with the conclusion stated by the hon. member for Medicine Hat. I might refer to the clear statement made by my colleague the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration.

DEBATES	September 1, 1966
There is no doubt that over the two years they are going to get at least 18 per cent. There is not the slightest doubt about that. What is bothering us is this. I have had discussions with several union leaders, and in commenting on the Munroe formula some of them expressed the thought that in collective bargaining with or without a mediator, or in further discussion, they would like to be free to consider changes in that 4-4-4-G formula. For example, they might want it to be 5 and 5 or 6 and 4.
This amendment, which is based on precedents established by the St. Laurent government in 1950 and by the Diefenbaker government in 1958, puts in the provisional amount and leaves it open to the parties to negotiate further. The unions themselves have stressed the desirability of flexibility, the possibility of changing the percentages to be found in the bill.
However, in deference to the reasoned approach of the hon. member for Medicine Hat, and because I believe the situation he envisages can be covered more effectively in an amendment to clause 10 rather than to the clause now under consideration, I will be quite willing to make a suggestion. Let the parties mediate. Let them continue to negotiate, and if they wish to vary these things by negotiation, let them be free to do so. But the suggested amendment makes it clear that if arbitration becomes necessary there will be nothing less.
I suggest that we stand clause 6 for the time being, and I shall ask the law officers and the officials of my department to give this further study. I would even be pleased to have the hon. member for Medicine Hat discuss the matter with them. I believe that we must give the parties flexibility, if they decide by genuine collective bargaining that they would like to vary these terms, while at the same time making it clear that if it comes to arbitration nothing less than 18 per cent will be granted.

Then we have had the innovation of centralized traffic control on Canadian National Railways. This is another example of technological change. Telegraph operators became redundant. There was a lengthy debate. The quotations from the debate of August 30, 1950, were repeated in that debate. Mr. St. Laurent spoke and toward the end of his speech he said:
The matters remaining in dispute were left for the arbitrator.
Listen to this sentence:
I may say I thought that, with our example before him, he might decide to treat them all on the same footing, but it was a matter that had to be determined by him. I believe it would be wrong for the government to ask parliament to vary the decision at which he arrived.
There, Mr. Chairman, was Mr. St. Laurent, eminent prime minister that he was, saying that because parliament had not written into the law what he thought would be the interpretation the arbitrator would accept there was nothing that we could then do about it.


I submit, Mr. Chairman, that we will find
ourselves in the same position with respect to the whole question of automation and technological change if we do not put some clear direction into the statute. The only direction that is there now is that the parties when they negotiate must consider all of the matters in dispute, including automation. The only direction there now is that the board of arbitration, if one is set up, must consider among other things the question of automation. But that board of arbitration, having considered the matter, can make no recommendation whatever. Therefore a matter in dispute, one of the reasons that this parliament was called into session, will not have been resolved satisfactorily.
We are right back where we were, Mr. Chairman, with respect to the question of wages. Moral guarantees do not have the effect in this kind of situation that words in a statute have. Mr. St. Laurent learned that in 1950 and 1951. I would have hoped that this government would show that it had learned that lesson.
I say to the Minister of Labour that I support the amendment moved by the hon. member for Nickel Belt but I would be happy, as I am sure he would, to accept some other kind of wording. I would also be happy to have the wording put into some other clause, and the minister himself might come up with something more appropriate. I think it would be quite satisfactory if there were somewhere a direction to the board of arbitration to write into the collective agreements an implementation of the principles of the Freedman report in appropriate language.
In other words, we do not ask that the precise terms of the agreement be provided here, although my hon. friend has given guidelines which could be followed. But we do think it is not satisfactory just to say that the matters in dispute are referred to the arbitrator. This will not cover automation and technological change any more than the same wording covered the wage issue. I urge the minister to take this question very seriously. I think he will find that to some of the employees who are now out on strike this is a more serious issue than the issue of wages. The whole question of this bill being palatable at all does depend on some satisfactory dealing with this important phase of the matter.
Because the minister at the end of his remarks on the substance of this amendment raised a point of order-I do not know
September 1. 1966	COMMONS
whether it was a tentative effort on his part or whether he meant it seriously-I would like to remind him that when we were on second reading and sought to move various amendments having to do with the Freedman report the Minister of National Health and Welfare argued that the place to do this was when we were in committee of the whole on the bill. This is something which we have been through hundreds of times in this house. When we are on second reading the government tells us to wait until we get into committee of the whole, and when we get into committee of the whole the government tells us no, this is not the place either.
I submit that the government and the Minister of Labour have been arguing that the phrase "all matters in dispute" in the legislation covers automation and technological change, so that this idea does not go beyond the scope of the bill. The whole purpose of the bill is to deal with the issues which brought on the strike. One of those issues was technological change. The minister admitted that time and time again by saying that this was one of the matters in dispute. Therefore, because it is part of what is before us I submit that it is within the four corners of this legislation and that it is definitely in order to move this amendment.
I repeat-and I know from conversation with my hon. friend for Nickel Belt that he does not object to my saying this-that the hon. member would be willing to have some alternative form of amendment. But it is certainly not satisfactory to ask the workers to go back to work without any guarantee that anything will be done about the question of automation and technological change other than those questions being discussed. Moral guarantees, a desire that it should happen -these things are not good enough, as Mr. St. Laurent learned in 1950 and 1951. We think that the importance of this matter requires that there be appropriate reference to it in the legislation itself.

Further, the preamble to the bill states among other things that the purpose and principle of this measure is to deal with the final settlement of terms and conditions of employment for the years 1966 and 1967. In the light of these words it seems to me we can introduce matters which deal with terms and conditions of employment, and job security certainly falls within this category.
While I do not agree with the wording of this amendment I believe we must certainly defend the right of the hon. member for Nickel Belt to introduce it and have it discussed. There can be no argument that a private member cannot move an amendment of this kind in connection with the bill before us on the ground that this is a money bill and so on. There is no superior competence in the hands of a minister. Any hon. member can move amendments of this kind.
There is, however, one difficulty which I see arising in connection with this amendment. The hon. member talks about the power of a conciliation board as set out in section 22(2) "of the act". But he does not say which act he has in mind. I think he means the Industrial

Legislation Respecting Railway Matters Relations and Disputes Investigation Act. However, the amendment does not say so. For this reason it is defective and the hon. member might wish to take it back and revise it accordingly.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I offered my submission on the point of order when I was speaking on the substance of this proposal, but may I say in reply to the Solicitor General, who objects to this amendment on the ground that it seeks to amend what he calls the statute law of the country, that the whole bill varies the provisions of the statute law, particularly in reference to the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act. Indeed, we do this all the time. Laws have an effect on each other, and merely to say that this amendment has an effect on some other statute does not make it out of order.
The hon. gentleman made one error in substance on this point when he said this amendment would apply to everything to which the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act applies. Not at all. It would apply the recommendations of the Freedman report only to the railway industry, as is made clear by the way in which this amendment is prepared and by the definitions in the statute.
In addition, as the hon. member for Medicine Hat has pointed out, if, as the minister says, it would be appropriate to move an amendment of this kind at some other place in the bill, then surely it would be appropriate to move it at any point so far as the rights of hon. members are concerned.

Perhaps I should reply to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre on this point of order. In the first place, no one on this side of the house said in my hearing that an amendment of this kind could be moved to any part of the bill. What was said was that the subject matter could be

dealt with elsewhere. That is a very different thing.
My hon. friend the Solicitor General said that this amendment goes beyond the principle and scope of the bill as established by the vote on second reading. It certainly does, because the scope of the bill was the resumption of the operation of the railways and this amendment seeks to import into the collective agreement which the bill asks us to establish the right to strike during the course of that agreement.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman-

I listened patiently to the hon. member. Perhaps he will listen to me now and reply later if he wishes. Further, this amendment seeks to set aside-I do not say to amend-the ordinary law which applies to every other collective agreement under the I.R.D.I.A. It purports to dispense with the normal law and establish a special law.
What is wrong with that?

That might be all right, if it had been part of the principles and scope of the bill before second reading. In that case, of course, it would have been possible to do this. But this proposal seeks to alter the bill as established on second reading and in this respect I suggest it is beyond the scope of the legislation passed by the house, in consequence of which this committee does not have competence to change the rules which have been laid down. speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
I apologize to the minister for having interrupted him. I was only about to ask him a question. Now he has sat down I will change it from a question to a statement. He said, without anything in his hand to help him make sure he was speaking correctly, that the purpose of this bill was to achieve a resumption of the operation of the railways. If he would pick up the bill and read the title on the front page he would find it says:
An act to provide for the resumption of operations of railways and for the settlement of the existing dispute with respect to terms and conditions of employment between railway companies and their employees.
If he will read the preamble he will find that the purpose is set out again. Let me read

the third paragraph of the preamble. It reads in part as follows:

-having regard to the interests of the railway-companies and the employees, provision be made for terms and conditions of employment for the year 1966, for the resumption of the processes of negotiation and mediation and for the final settlement of terms and conditions of employment for the years 1966 and 1967.
When we get into the body of the bill we find references to disputes, and this has been quoted time and time again by the Minister of Labour. In other words, I rest my case on the very point that the minister makes, namely, that we have to be in committee of the whole within the scope of the bill that was given passage on second reading. But the minister put in only half of the scope, which is to get the railways running again. The other half is to settle the matters in dispute. The minister does not argue that disputes are not included. Therefore I submit the amendment meets the test that the Minister of Transport has raised, namely, that it is within the scope of the legislation agreed to on second reading.

If I may reply to that, since it has become a question, my reply is very simple. The purpose of the bill, as the hon. gentleman said, is to get the railways running again and settle the dispute. To seek to import into the bill a clause stating that once operations were resumed a further strike could be allowed to start a week later is totally contrary to the decision made. If we want to import that kind of principle into the general law of Canada with respect to collective agreements, that is another matter, but to make a special and different law for this one group of collective agreements would make it possible to have another national crisis, which would be a very odd way of carrying out the decision parliament has made on second reading. It is true that dispute is covered in the bill, but for us to seek to import this kind of clause into it seems to be not only beyond the scope of the bill but to be contrary to the purpose of the bill.

Mr. Chairman, what we in the opposition have been trying to do since Monday is to bring about a bill that will be effective, with justice and equity. I am trying to view this matter from the point of national interest and from a desire not to bring about legislation that will have dangers for the future inherent in it.
I have pressed the government to place pro.
visions in this bill to implement the Freedman

Legislation Respecting Railway Matters report. Within the last hour I have spoken to railway men, reasonable, responsible, rational men who want to do what is good for Canada. One of the things that they impressed on me is that it is going to be very difficult to secure adherence to the law unless something is done about the implementation of the Freedman report.
I am told the report is a best seller in the office of the Queen's Printer. It has become a standard work for employees and employers. Once more I advance this prayer for relief out of a desire to assure that whatever legislation is passed will not run the danger and possibility of not being followed.
I believe there should be a material amendment to cover the Freedman report or certain of its recommendations, but let us read this amendment and see what it means. Surely parliament is not going to pass an amendment to change the labour law of Canada to apply to one industry and to bring about the benevolent attitude that is inherent in this amendment. At the expense of taking up time I want to read the amendment which states:
Notwithstanding the provisions of any other act, the terms and conditions of each collective agreement to which this act applies are amended forthwith by inserting therein the following clause:
"The employer shall not introduce or implement any technological innovation, development, or change which would materially and adversely affect the working conditions of his employees until after he has negotiated the matter with the bargaining agent of his employees, and that if no agreement is reached, the matter shall be referred to a conciliation board as provided by section 22(2) of the act-"
I am not arguing the merits at the moment, but up to that point if the amendment were accepted it would be along the line that I advocated this morning. It is the next portion that I do not think parliament can possibly accept.
I want to see fairness and equity to the men who work. I do not have to provide references about fairness and equity to the men of the railways because I acted for them on more than one occasion without fee. Indeed, I was called to the bar of the province of British Columbia to defend a railroad man without fee and had to pay admission to the bar of that province. On that occasion it cost me $1,500 to be called to the bar in order to take the case of a man who was unable to pay legal fees.

Would the right hon. gentleman permit a comment? I want to congratulate him for undertaking legal work on behalf of union members for which he did not receive a fee.

-and that if the employer introduces or implements the proposed changes without such negotiation and conciliation his employees shall have the right to strike immediately-

-as if the collective agreement had expired and all other statutory requirements had been met.

To accept this amendment would be something that this House of Commons dare not do.
Having said that, again I come back to the question regarding the Freedman commission.

My opinion as a person who has read statutes is that I think what is meant by the words "amended as provided by this act" is that they refer not only to clause 6 but also to any amendments made by virtue of the machinery set up in clauses 8, 9 and 10. Legislation Respecting Railway Matters clause 6. I am not saying I agree with that interpretation. I am saying that the words as they now are interpreted by some people would be limited to clause 6. Mr. Chairman, I indicated this morning that I intended to move an amendment which I think, if accepted, will go a long way toward bringing about a sense of unity in our country in regard to carrying out the law. I am not going to traverse the ground I have already covered.
I have been quite interested in discussions I have had with railroaders as to the changes they would like to have effected in order to remove certain inconveniences. If these objections are not met they will ultimately lead to a sense of resentment and frustration. Let me advance two examples, the first of which involves a very small matter. Many railroaders have expressed to me the desire to have the pay days changed from twice monthly to every other Thursday. Such a change would actually cost very little. The total cost, according to estimates I have received, would be approximately $40,000 to $50,000. I am also informed that the wives of these railroaders are in favour of this change. From the vertical manner in which the hon. member for Verdun has moved his head, and he has made a study of this situation, I can only conclude that he agrees that this is a small matter of some importance.
The other example I wish to present deals with the health and welfare plan in respect of which there is a general feeling today that


if the railway companies were to absorb or pay the employees half it would be most acceptable. This would be a benefit to the employees and it would be non-taxable. Those are the kinds of things which, being now neglected, result in an accumulation of feelings that borders on resentment.
Everywhere I go railwaymen ask why the Freedman report has been left in cold storage. While it is true that it is being considered, that consideration has carried on for a long time. If we in this parliament were by statute, rather than by verbal declaration or vocal support, to add a clause which indicated that the Freedman report was going to receive not only consideration but action we would be going a long way toward assuring that the railway employees, when this bill passes parliament, will accept it and return to work.
I do not intend to press these things further, but hon. members know my feelings in this regard. I do suggest that unless we in parliament, with a deep sense of responsibility, provide something of a definite nature in respect of adopting the recommendations of the Freedman report, these men who are on strike will feel that we have deprived them of their right to collective bargaining by substituting compulsory arbitration. I ask the minister-I know he is very fair in the manner in which he endeavours to solve the problems that come under his jurisdiction-whether he will not recommend to the government the acceptance of an amendment along these lines:
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
That clause 8 be amended by substituting a comma for the period in line 11 and the following words be added:
"and that part of the collective bargaining to be undertaken will include provision for discussion and negotiation between the railways and the unions concerning the work changes, elimination of jobs, and general working conditions that may be affected by the introduction of technological and other changes."
That is not an arbitrary amendment; it is an amendment designed to bring about cooperation on the part of those concerned with the strike. I believe the cost of the strike is $15 million a day. When the men go back to work under law we want them to do so in the spirit that they have shown on so many occasions throughout the years.
This opinion is not based on personal observation. It is based on discussions I have had with responsible leaders of the labour movement and telephone conversations across this country in the last several days. I worked on this amendment during the night,
September 1, 1966

trying to bring about something that, if the house will accept it, will mean that we can all be united, as I see it, in this house and parliament can speak with the authority of unity.
That is what we started to effect. We brought about changes. We had to fight for them, but having fought for them changes were made. I will make no further appeal during this debate. The minister must know the festering disquietude of the men on the railways because of the failure up to the present time to implement this report. If the workers across Canada know now that when operations have begun the discussions and negotiations that take place will cover this field, we will go a long, long way toward bringing about that mutual trust without which no law passed by parliament can ever be effective if it is one that is coercive, determinant and ends rights. On the one hand we have the national interest and on the other the rights of free men to have in their work those amenities that most of us have.

Mr. Chairman, it seems to me that while the Leader of the Official Opposition has done very well in posing the problems which have arisen in the railway industry as a result of rapid technological changes and the tremendous effect these have had on the lives of railway workers, this amendment really adds nothing at all to clause 8 because that clause already says:
The railway companies and unions shall forthwith enter into negotiations with a view to the settlement of any matters presently in dispute-
The Leader of the Opposition suggests that we add as an amendment, "that part of the collective bargaining to be undertaken will include provision for discussion and negotiation." This amendment restates what clause 8 already says. In years gone by there has been plenty of discussion among the companies and the unions. The reason we have had these difficulties, the reason for the stoppage at Nakina and the stoppage of the whole railway system was that the railways and the unions concerned could not reach agreement. When they could not reach agreement, and when the railway companies insisted on exercising what they considered to be their right to manage the system and to make changes unilaterally, the men exercised what they considered to be their right to stop work, to withdraw from service. I remember that the former minister of transport, now the house leader, when he was warned by the former
DEBATES	7969
Legislation Respecting Railway Matters member for Port Arthur that there would be a stoppage, brushed aside that warning. The minister said he had been told by the president of Canadian National Railways that there were no problems. They were certain they could put through this change and the men would accept it. Then we were faced that week end with virtually a complete stoppage of the C.N.R. system.
The reason this matter has to be solved now, I am convinced, the reason it cannot be put off, the reason it cannot be left to later negotiation and we must include in the bill a clause to cover the situation, although probably not the amendment moved a little earlier by my colleague from Nickel Belt and not this amendment because I do not think it is acceptable, is that it is quite conceivable-I am not suggesting for a moment that I speak for the railway workers because they have not authorized me to do so and I am not their spokesman, but I know railway workers-in my opinion that the bill as now drafted, with the changes proposed to clause 6, will be acceptable to a large number of railway workers. I am thinking of the monetary proposals contained in the bill.
However, the operating employees, particularly the members of the Brotherhood of Railroad Trainmen, are insistent and determined that changes be made which will guarantee them the rights which Mr. Justice Freedman expressed so eloquently in his report. I have an amendment to propose to this clause, Mr. Chairman. It is a very simple one and I offer it in the spirit of the suggestion made by the Prime Minister last night that if this legislation could be improved it should be improved. My amendment would simply substitute the word "October" for the word "November" in the clause. The clause now reads:
The Minister of Labour shall appoint a mediator or mediators (hereinafter referred to as the
Legislation Respecting Railway Matters "mediator") who shall forthwith endeavour to mediate the matters in dispute between the railway companies and the unions and to bring about agreement between them and who shall report to the Minister of Labour, not later than November 15, 1966-
My amendment would substitute the words "October 15, 1966".
-on the progress of the negotiations between the railway companies and the unions.
The purpose of my amendment is to deal with one of the very serious grievances felt by the members of the railway unions with respect to this legislation. They have considerable doubt in their minds, from experience, about the value of continued negotiations as provided for by clause 8 with which we have just dealt. I hope they are wrong. I have heard various members of the government express the view that they are wrong in assuming that because compulsory arbitration is proposed by clause 10 the process of mediation and negotiation contemplated in clauses 8 and 9 will not have effective results.
Let me put it both ways. Suppose the result is successful. Surely this parliament should impart a sense of urgency to the mediation proceedings. I do not believe we impart any sense of urgency if we suggest that mediation proceedings should continue until November 15, 1966 That would cover a total of roughly ten weeks. I am aware, as all hon. members are, that there are complex issues to be decided. If the mediation proposals are given that spirit of urgency which the situation demands, then there is every reasonable prospect that negotiations can be concluded within the six weeks period the amendment would propose.
On the other hand, Mr. Chairman, if this process of negotiation is to be long drawn out and unsuccessful, as some of the union members feel from past experience, then it is just another exacerbating delay in the final solution of this matter. One of the great difficulties with labour relations, as anyone experienced in them knows, is the long periods of delay before decisions are finally made. I think it was my leader who referred to the ritualistic dance. Ritualistic dances may be all very well and they may be necessary, but they get tiresome if they are drawn out month after month.
I suggest it would greatly add to the attractiveness of this bill-I do not say it is too attractive-in the minds of those who are on strike if we provided evidence in the bill of a sense of urgency which is not in the legislation at the moment. Someone may say there
7972	COMMONS
Legislation Respecting Railway Matters is a possibility that by October 15 these negotiations may have made admirable progress and yet be just short of a conclusive result at that date and that it would be a great mistake to dash suddenly into compulsory arbitration when real progress had been made. I agree, and I point out that that situation is adequately covered by subclause 2 which enables an extension of time if the mediator reports favourable progress. It may seem a small matter to substitute October for November, but I think it would be a symptom of the fact this house is ready to try to impart a sense of urgency to the negotiations. This is one of the grievances that has been in the minds of many workers. I know this from speaking to them. They feel this process has been delayed and delayed. Therefore I move:

Mr. Chairman, speaking for this group may I say that we are not in support of the proposed amendment. We feel that now parliament has met reasonable time must be given. There is now a completely different set of circumstances confronting the people who are going to negotiate, and it is only fair to give them a little time to do their work and enable them to come up with something that they themselves have produced instead of having mandatory arbitration. Therefore we in this group are not prepared to support the amendment.

Mr. Chairman, there is no doubt about the urgency of this matter, but another very important principle is involved so far as the government is concerned and I am sure so far as the great majority of the members of this house are concerned.
All of us have said more than once, and said sincerely, that we believe in collective bargaining. During the past eight or nine days I have had the opportunity of meeting with the union leaders, sometimes for a few moments and on occasion for an hour or more in a session. I have some idea of the multitude and complexity of the issues which have to be dealt with. A study of the Freedman report is only one good example. If we are going to bring finality to this matter, the success of the mediation proceedings will depend to a large extent upon the man chosen as mediator.
I have given considerable thought to this question and I have discussed with my colleagues the person who I feel could do the

best job. While I cannot appoint any such person until the proposed bill has become law, because of the urgency which exists we would be dilatory in our duty if we did not canvas the possibility of getting the man we consider most competent for this job before he became tied up with other commitments. We would want him to start as soon as possible and continue the efforts of negotiation and mediation.
The bill has been drawn with this in mind, and it is not necessary for the mediator or mediators to wait until November 15 before considering the matter. To one listening to the hon. member for Greenwood that might be the conclusion. The bill is deliberately drawn to make provision for this situation. What the clause says is:
The Minister of Labour shall appoint a mediator or mediators (hereinafter referred to as the "mediator") who shall forthwith endeavour to mediate the matters in dispute between the railway companies and the unions and to bring about agreement between them and who shall report to the Minister of Labour-
Then the bill does not say on November 15 but "not later than November 15". If the mediator reports that the negotiations are fruitless, then he does not have to wait until November 15; that would be absurd. We have in mind as the mediator a man who, if this bill is passed, will I am sure meet with-I cannot say unanimous acceptance-the overwhelming support of this committee. That reason is that as soon as this measure has been accepted by the house, if it is, it is my intention, as has already been indicated by the first reading given to the bill, to introduce legislation which, notwithstanding the observations made earlier today by the hon. member for York South, the government believes will have the effect of giving the railways greater freedom to conduct their operations in a way which we hope, believe

and expect will give them reason to feel, not right away of course but during the course of 1967, that they are in a better position to bargain successfully with their workers without imposing as a background another direct charge upon the taxpayers of Canada.
I do not dissent from the position expressed earlier today by the hon. member for York South that there are some kinds of transportation services that the railways are expected to provide. I am not seeking to debate the bill but, just as an illustration of the reasons for the desirability of this delay, in the bill we are asking parliament to authorize a proper costing of these services that are performed by the railways for national, public or social reasons.
The railways will know that they are going to be remunerated by the taxpayers for these services, and I think that this is a good and sound principle. It is not fair to put a charge on other shippers just because the railways are compelled by parliament to perform unremunerative services which are socially or economically desirable for the rest of the community. That was the principle which was enunciated. This means that the railways will know more certainly that they will be remunerated for these services and that the remuneration will be properly calculated. They will be able to count on that.
I think it is also most desirable that those services which could and should be remunerative and which are comptetitive should be run in a businesslike way instead of becoming a drain upon the taxpayers. But until the railways are in a position to conduct their business as other carriers are permitted to conduct theirs, they are not in an adequate position to bargain effectively.
I realize that this other measure is not going to get through the house between today and tomorrow. Indeed, it would be shocking if parliament were to adopt it within that short space of time. Nevertheless I hope that we will proceed with all due expedition and give the bill passage, possibly with some amendment, even though this will take some weeks. These things will be going forward at the same time as this period is running.
I feel that if the collective bargaining and mediation provided for in this bill are to have any kind of meaning, negotiations must go on beyond the reasonably anticipated period for the final passage of this legislation. The railway companies will then know what are the circumstances in which they are operating

Mr. Chairman, having listened to the Minister of Transport I am in a position to realize how proper the amendment is. As he went on to list all the difficulties it became obvious to me that if we must wait to assess all the benefits which will flow to the companies from the complicated legislation we are to deal with here, the mediation will be protracted long after October 15 or even November 15.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, without
agreeing to the desirability of having clause 10 at all I should like to move another amendment, and in doing so I invite the committee to return seriously and sympathetically to the question of the Freedman report recommendations.
It has been agreed on all sides that this matter can be discussed during the negotiations which will follow the passing of this bill and that they can be gone into if necessary by the board of arbitration. The Minister of Labour and some of his colleagues have given an assurance that this is what they want done. I am still conscious of what happened in 1950 when Mr. St. Laurent wanted something done which Mr. Justice Kellock felt the act did not give him authority to do. But we are agreed that one of the issues in dispute is
September 1, 1966

Legislation Respecting Railway Matters the question of technological change and that it is one which can come under consideration.
We feel, and in this I think we are expressing a view held very strongly by the workers who are out on strike, that it is not good enough just to have the assurance that this matter will be discussed. There should be some assurance that action will be taken. The government has already accepted the proposition put forward both inside and outside the house that it was not good enough to leave the issue of wage rates for 1967 merely as something to be discussed. It was felt there should be some floor. We suggest it is similarly not good enough to leave this other issue, this burning issue, merely as one the discussion of which is guaranteed.
I remind the committee that this matter has been discussed at length for a long time. Judge Robinson, chairman of the conciliation board in 1962, urged that the problem be placed before parliament and dealt with by legislation. In 1962 the Brotherhood of Railroad Trainmen, and perhaps others, asked for an industrial inquiry commission to go into this issue. There was a wildcat strike on the C.N.R. in 1964. There was the Freedman report on November 17, 1965, the terms and recommendations of which have become almost a bible, referred to time and time again.
Then there is the report of Judge Little who headed one of the boards in the current dispute, a report in which legislation by parliament was recommended. How many times does this matter have to be discussed and put to arbitration before some action is taken? I say again that this is one of the most important issues involved. It is just as serious as the wage issue. Indeed, for many it is even more serious.
Whether we approve or not, parliament has grappled with the wage issue and I recognize that parliament must deal with this matter if it expects the men to go back to work. We urge the government to recognize that this other issue is just as serious and, to many of the employees, more serious. We have had discussion of this matter on other clauses. Discussion took place on the amendment which the hon. member for Nickel Belt put before the committee and later withdrew. It took place on the amendment proposed by the Leader of the Opposition. So it is not necessary to carry on at length.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
But I dare to suggest that as a result of what has already been said we have come up

with another amendment that meets some of the objections made and which I seriously ask the minister and the Prime Minister to consider. When I asked my hon. friend to withdraw his previous amendment I read the wording of another one which I had drafted. Since then I have tried to improve that draft and am prepared to move it as an amendment inserting a new subclause 1 (c) in clause 10.
As clause 10 is constructed it sets out a provision for what the government may do after a mediator has reported. In other words, under clause 8 we accept the fact that in their negotiations the parties can discuss the Freedman report, and if they come up with an agreement that is fine and nothing more needs to be done. But the whole purport of clause 10 is to give the government power under regulation by order in council to take whatever steps may be necessary if satisfactory conclusions are not reached under clauses 8 and 9.
We suggest that if the point is reached where the mediator reports there is no agreement on the question of the Freedman recommendations, then the government should have the authority to instruct the board of arbitration to deal with that issue. At the point I have mentioned I believe the government should have power by order in council to put this matter in the hands of the board of arbitration with a guideline or minimum standard that must be met. Therefore to meet this condition and improve the bill in one of its main deficiencies I move:
That clause 10 be amended by inserting therein, immediately after subclause (b) of clause (1) thereof, the following new subclause (c):
"(c) instructing the board to determine and provide in an appropriate form, an amendment to the collective agreements to which this act applies implementing the recommendations of the report of the Industrial Inquiry Commission on Canadian National Railways Run-Throughs, dated November 17, 1965."
This amendment does not write in detail the terms of such an item for a collective agreement. It does not include anything which might offend the Leader of the Opposition, as did the previous one. It leaves it to the board of arbitration to draft the amendment to the collective agreements, but just as we have set a floor under wages, so it sets a minimum that must be met. That minimum would be an inclusion in the collective agreements of an appropriate form of the recommendations of the Freedman report.
September 1, 1966

I recognize the earnestness with which the Minister of Labour has dealt with the problem of automation and technological change.
I recognize that he found it not very pleasant to oppose the amendment to clause 8 moved by the Leader of the Opposition. I feel he wants to deal with this matter, and just as the government has accepted the proposition of a floor with respect to wages I suggest it should accept the proposition that there be a minimum so far as automation and technological changes are concerned.
When the government agreed to the floor under wage rates in 1967 and to the 18 per cent total package it made its bill a little more palatable and acceptable to many of the workers, but there are many of them who also consider this a serious point and to whom the bill would be a lot more palatable if they knew that as the result of the negotiations and arbitration that may yet take place something will be done about this important question. I urge the minister to consider the amendment sympathetically.

Mr. Chairman, in view of the observations that I made earlier when commenting on the persuasive arguments advanced by the Leader of the Opposition, and in view of the firm assurance I gave hon. members that in the instructions to the mediator and, if necessary, the eventual instructions to the board of arbitration, we would direct specific and urgent attention to the technological change problem as dealt with in the Freedman report, I see no necessity for this amendment. The position is quite clear, and for that reason we oppose this amendment.

Of course I listened to the hon. member for York South, but the circumstances in this case are entirely different. Mr. Justice Kellock was appointed an industrial commissioner under the provisions of the
