Legislation Respecting Railway Matters Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act. This bill, if passed, authorizes the Minister of Labour to appoint a mediator, and I have undertaken to give that mediator specific instructions.

Apparently we have failed to make our point clear to the minister. Two things can be done. One is that the minister in his advice or instructions to the board of arbitrators may say, "You are hereby instructed to deal with this matter." I have no doubt in the world that the minister will do that. He has given an assurance that he intends to tell the board of arbitration to deal with the matter of the Freedman report, but I respectfully suggest to him that that means the board of arbitration would then be considering precisely the same things as Mr. Justice Freedman considered. I can again go over the ground in respect of the need for it and how to implement it.
On the other hand, there is another thing which can be done; that is, that the minister be given authority by this parliament to say to the board of arbitration, "You are not merely to deal with this matter, but you are to come up with certain actual clauses in the collective agreement implementing the recommendations of the Freedman report". The minister refuses to recognize the obvious and important distinctions between the two. His assurance-and I use the term with the reservation which I am sure the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre does-so long as it is not in the bill, amounts to no more than an assurance that he will tell the board to deal with it. The board may decide to do nothing about it. There is nothing in the law which requires that it be done. If you want, as you do, to assuage the fears the workers have on this point and make clear that something definite will in fact be done, then this is the way to do it. I say to the minister as emphatically as I can that his assurance, sincerely given and accepted by this house, is not of the slightest value in this situation, because his assurance can go no further than ask for more discussion and more deliberation. What the workers, and particularly the Brotherhood of Railway Trainmen, require is an assurance in this act that the Freedman recommendation
7976	COMMONS
Legislation Respecting Railway Matters will be implemented in an appropriate form, decided upon either by the mediation board or, if mediation fails, by the board of arbitrators. That assurance can be there only if it is written into the bill.
I say to the government, as did the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, that this is just as important as the wages. A few moments ago I was called out of this chamber and informed, not by a member of the committee with which the minister met, but by a lawyer for the Brotherhood of Railway Trainmen, that he has been on the telephone with the union office and has been informed that this question of assurance in the bill that the Freedman report be implemented is of the utmost importance to his members who now are on strike.
There is no reason that this could not be done. How many more times must we investigate this problem. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has indicated how many times this has been before tribunals. It was before a board in 1962, and then there was the wildcat strike in 1965. Mr. Justice Freedman made a thorough investigation and report. There was a committee of the house some years ago which came to the same conclusion. Surely we have had enough inquiries and investigations. Mr. Chairman, clause 10 of Bill No. C-230 deals with compulsory arbitration and we can find in subclause (2) that:
(2) In the event that a board of arbitrators Is appointed under paragraph (a) of subsection (1) and decides any matter not agreed upon between a railway company and a union at the time of its decision, the collective agreement to which this act applies between the railway company and the union shall be deemed to be amended by the incorporation therein of such decision-

Yesterday, we had comments on, and opposition to, this compulsory arbitration, from certain leaders. For my part, I put the question to the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) last night, as recorded in the right-hand column of page 7848 of the official report:
In the name of the freedom of the workingmen on the railways, or of any workingmen in Canada, the hon. member is strongly opposed to compulsory arbitration. Would he also be opposed, for the same reason, to the compulsory check-off which is entirely against freedom of any workingman who does not want to belong to any union in Canada?
The answer of the hon. member for York South, as recorded in the left-hand column of page 7849 was as follows:
In my own opinion it is not, and I therefore support deduction of union dues.
He did not say compulsory dues or deductions. I had put before him the question of compulsory deductions.
Now, Mr. Chairman, among the objections we receive, we could read a communication issued by the president of the Canadian Labour Congress in a press release dated August 30. He said:
The proposed legislation to end the Canadian railroad workers' strike is a coercive measure
[The Deputy Chairman.]

which is to the credit neither of the government that introduced it, nor, if it should be passed, of Canada. Its major objective is to coerce free men into working against their will-
Mr. Chairman, when I see such a statement by a labour leader with Mr. Jodoin's standing, I can but question the sincerity of such a man. When we refer to union check-off and compulsory dues and we object to them, Mr. Jodoin and other labour leaders claim foul play and cry democracy. It should be remembered that the Canadian railroad workers have stopped working quite legally, there is no question about that. But they are being placed in a position of having to choose between compulsion and refusal to submit to legislation they know is bad.
Mr. Chairman, in the case of the Canadian railroads, as the minister is aware, the unions, whichever they were, forced the government and the employers to deduct compulsory union dues to such a point that a railroad employee may not even keep his job if he fails to pay his union dues, if he fails to go to a certain bank when he gets his pay and his union dues are not paid up, he loses his job, not because he is fired by the company that hired him, but because the union boss decides that such a worker is no longer entitled to work, precisely because he has failed to pay his compulsory dues.
The worker is no longer entitled to work, precisely because he has failed to pay his compulsory dues to the union.
Mr. Chairman, it is time such hypocrisy is bared, that such notorious hypocrisy is revealed to Canadian workers who are being exploited by such people.
When we mention compulsory arbitration, the people of the New Democratic Party rise against the notion; it is a direct attack on union freedom; but when the unions force workers to join the union in order to be entitled to earn their daily bread, is that no longer dictatorship? Is this respect for personal freedom?
Mr. Chairman, I am also against compulsory arbitration; I am against compulsory union dues; I am against income tax deducted at the source from workers' pay cheques.
I want a worker who earns $100 to get $100; let him spend his earnings as he sees fit; let him pay his union dues himself; let him pay his income tax himself; let him pay himself for what he wants or what he expects from the economic or social life of his country. But when I see labour leaders writing to us
September 1, 1966

-like this one from the Canadian Brotherhood of Railway, Transport and General Workers, London, Ontario, did on August 30, 1966. What does Mr. Gallagher, secretary of that organization have to say?

-that the leaders of the federal political parties in Canada be advised of our complete opposition to compulsory arbitration, or any legislation aimed at forcing us-
The unions.
-to accept anything less than a settlement of all our demands, on a basis acceptable to a majority of our members across Canada.

Union freedom is increased, I agree, but freedom of the individual is sabotaged at its base. This, Mr. Chairman, is to show that I would object to clause 10 if union leaders were ready to forget compulsory union deductions. I would object to that myself but if union leaders want compulsory measures in order to force people to work according to the dictates of certain union leaders, Mr. Chairman, then I will vote in favour of clause 10 which calls for, orders, and recommends compulsory arbitration.
When we see these compulsory measures right and left-I was reading a circular the other day put out in the province of Quebec by some of my old friends, staff members of the paper titled Vers Demain, which stated:
Why all these strikes? Actual reasons:
Give unions importance and power; put families out in the street; ruin landlords and businessmen; hinder police protection; create general dissatisfaction, forerunner of revolution; promote class struggles, in all spheres, including religion; stir up an atmosphere of confusion, favourable to revolutionary action; enable revolutionaries to carry out riot exercises; actually launch communist revolution; have the enemies of revolution thrown in prison, under the pretext of protecting the public.
This same Vers Demain paper stated last month:
We demand that the Quebec parliament take five necessary measure toward the recovery of public freedom and security;
1.	Abolition of compulsory union contribution.
This is what unions are asking parliament or government to take out of its bill No. C-230, to delete "compulsory" from the bill.
2.	Abolition of the right to strike in the public services.
When we had a strike in the hospitals of the province, Mr. Chairman, do you think what happened was something to be proud of, letting people out of hospitals because some union leaders in the province of Quebec had
Legislation Respecting Railway Matters decided that hospitals must close down? Old people turned into the street because the union leaders had decided to get them out of the hospitals. And the public authorities tolerate such a situation resulting precisely from the compulsory which those people demand to help themselves and not to serve the Canadian people.
3.	Picketing to be prohibited in all strikes.
4.	Hospitals to be handed back to private institutions, religious or medical.
Mr. Chairman, those are recommendations which the newspaper Vers Demain made throughout the province and I endorse them. I do not endorse everything that the people of Vers Demain do, but when it makes sense, when they fight for the respect due to man, I do. To respect an odourless, colourless, tasteless organization does not appeal to me.
But the people who are part of the organization, for instance, the human being, the worker, the farmer, the settler, the white-collar worker, the physician, the professional man, anyone deserves respect and no one, no labour leader has the right to go against the freedom of the individual. No one has the right to prevent a Canadian from earning an honest and decent living.
Within the unions that right is not recognized. If one does not belong to the union, he does not have the right to work; on top of this, you have to pay a premium to belong to the union. This was the practice in Sudbury and in Rouyn-Noranda. In fact, when men were sent from Rouyn to Sault Ste. Marie, the union charged $50 to $100 to allow a worker into the union. It was compulsory, a condition which a man had to accept in order to be allowed to earn his living.
Mr. Chairman, as I indicated in my press release, the time has come to unmask some of the union leaders. This does not mean that we are against the unions. I say to the people and the workers: belong to the unions, but control them.
When I meet railwaymen in Rouyn-Nor-anda working for the C.N.R. or the Ontario Northland Railway, they tell me: since we made union contributions compulsory, we have had no service from our union leaders. When union contributions are no longer compulsory, the union leaders will have to take care of the workers and serve their best interests, instead of exploiting them and allowing the situation to reach the point where parliament must be recalled to draw up a bill in order to try and force people to accept working conditions, and force the employers

Legislation Respecting Railway Matters to accept the unions' point of view, and so forth.
Mr. Chairman, when the Canadian economy is such that each individual can develop according to his aspirations, then we will hear no talk of compulsion, but of personal freedom, secure in the knowledge that Canada is able to take care of all its population.

Mr. Chairman, I hardly think the public and the house would understand if we were to take time out to reply to the diatribe of the hon. member for Ville-neuve (Mr. Caouette) woven of half-truths, misinformation and a certain number of prejudices dating back to the previous century.
Let us say, Mr. Chairman, that I only wish to indicate that, at the first opportunity, I shall try to reply point by point to the statements made by the hon. member for Villeneuve.

Mr. Chairman, I could always follow the hon. minister to give him a few pointers on the proprieties toward Canadian workers.

Mr. Chairman, I appreciate the fact that the committee would like to get through with this matter as quickly as possible, but I have an amendment to make which I make seriously because I believe it will improve the legislation, make it more workable and acceptable; and I believe furthermore that it is in accordance with the principles accepted by all quarters of this house. The amendment that I propose, Mr. Chairman, adopts as a basis or floor for negotiation and arbitration provided for by these subclauses of clause 10 the recommendations made by the chairman of the board of conciliation in matters other than wage issues. As is probably known to all hon. members of this house, Mr. Justice Munroe and Mr. Justice Cameron included in their recommendations not only the wage provisions which we have fully discussed in this house but a number of what have been described as fringe benefits. These recommendations included such matters as improvement in annual vacations, insurance and unemployment benefits, bereavement leave, statutory holidays and other matters of this sort.
One of the reasons for which this bill, when it was originally introduced, ran into such a hostile reception from many people, including those in the railway unions and the

people affected, was their belief that the effect of this bill was to take away even those favourable recommendations which had been approved by these conciliation boards. The reason for this hostility was not only the monetary issues which we have discussed and which may have been important, but also the feeling that these other matters which had been discussed at length and in a sense judicially determined as being appropriate were not once again to be made a subject of negotiation and taken away from them.
The argument has been made that these matters should be left to collective bargaining and arbitration. I agree with that, but if this matter goes to compulsory arbitration then I suggest that the very same principle applies here as has applied to what we have done with the wage issue. In the wage issue we have said that the basis, the floor or the foundation-I am using the words which have been used by ministers in this house- which the arbitration tribunal decided upon should not fall below the standard already judicially approved by the boards of conciliation.
The same thing was said in regard to wage proposals. We were told that we should leave the 1967 wages to conciliation, discussion, mediation and arbitration. This committee is well aware that in order to move toward making this bill acceptable we had to enunciate a principle, which was enunciated, that if we were truly to make the report to the board of conciliation a basis or foundation for any future settlement or for compulsory arbitration, a floor should at least be provided so that those benefits which were already recommended should not in effect be taken away.
It has been said in the house by the Prime Minister among others that parliament regrets having to intervene in matters of collective bargaining and labour relations, and that it should intervene as little as possible. This is true. However, if we have to intervene- and in this case we certainly must-then it would be folly, I suggest, not to intervene effectively on the basis of the principle that we must leave everything to conciliation and arbitration so as to secure the acquiescence if not the approval of those whose lives and working conditions are affected.
I am asking the Minister of Labour whether in this connection he subscribes to the argument that was so forcefully presented by the Minister of National Health and Welfare and the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration.
September 1, 1966

They said that the recommendations on future wages in the Munroe report, and I take it in the Cameron report, were, although not positively enacted, virtually certain to be acceptable or, to paraphrase the words of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, morally binding. For that reason they said that without explicit enactment in this legislation there was a basis, a foundation or a floor for future negotiation and arbitration. Does the minister also believe that on the other hand the railway companies will be free in the negotiation to refuse to include these recommendations, or that the arbitrator will be free to take away that which has already been recommended on the non-wage matters included in these reports?
I want to state with all the force I can that if the principle that we are adopting in this house is that we are intervening in this matter on the basis of the Munroe report and the conciliation board's report, and if we have found it necessary, as we have, to incorporate that report as a basic minimum below which negotiations will not go in respect of wages, precisely the same argument is applicable in respect of the so-called fringe benefits.
The word "fringe" somehow makes it sound as if these benefits were unimportant, but I assure you, Mr. Chairman, and the members of this committee that these arguments are not unimportant to those whose lives are directly affected. The acceptability of what parliament proposes to do here is affected by these matters. I want to know why we are asked to approve the proposition that the Munroe report shall set a floor in respect of wages, and not in regard to these other matters.

I therefore move, Mr. Chairman:
That clause 10 be amended by adding thereto paragraph 1(c) which will read as follows:
"Provided that if the decision referred to in paragraph 10(b) -
That is the decision of the board of arbitrators.
-is less favourable to the claims of the employees in respect of terms or conditions of employment than the recommendations made by chairmen of boards of conciliation in respect to collective agreements to which this act applies, then the said collective agreements shall be revised or amended so as to comply with the said recommendations.
This amendment is couched in legal language but the principle is simple. The principle is that if we are to have our legislation
based upon the reports of the justices, who
DEBATES	7981
Legislation Respecting Railway Matters have been praised as experts in this field, if we are going to make them the basis of our legislation upon which we are asking men to go back to work without being able to exercise the normal right to strike, then we must incorporate not part but all of those recommendations.
This applies to the non-wage as well as the wage benefits. This amendment is consistent with what the Leader of the Opposition so forcefully put before us, and is consistent with what the ministers themselves have said is the basis of this matter. The acceptance of this proposal will give a guarantee to the employees concerned that they will not have to renegotiate the items already recommended in their favour by the boards of conciliation. I urge the Prime Minister and the Minister of Labour, in view of what was said last night when they asked for improvements or suggestions to make this bill more acceptable, to accept this amendment. 1 want to assure them and other members of this house that if this is accepted it will be another thing that will make it simpler and easier for those who are in leadership within the unions to be able to say that this parliament has been fair. It has changed its mind and improved the original legislation. It has made the full basis of the Munroe report the floor below which, at any future time, they can not be forced by any lengthy negotiation or any compulsory arbitration.

I think I should speak but will do so very briefly. When this suggestion was put forward by the hon. member for Greenwood this morning I assured him and the committee that I would give it further consideration. I have done so. Mr. Chairman, I will wait for some of the noise to simmer down. I have not as yet had anything to say at any stage of the discussion of this bill, even though I recognize that the bill and the situation which brought it in is one of the most serious and important questions with which this parliament has been called upon to deal for some time.
The particular clause, clause 10, with which the committee is dealing at the present time seemed well on its way to becoming one of the most amended clauses of any bill which we have had for some time, or certainly is a clause to which many amendments have been sought to be attached. However I want to assure the committee that it is not my intention to propose any further amendment to this clause. Indeed, if it were possible within the rules what I would be rising to do would be to move for its complete elimination from the bill. However I recognize that under the rules it would not be in order for me to do this, and when the appropriate time comes I shall have the opportunity of expressing my views upon it by the way that I will vote when the vote is called.
I should like to draw to the attention of the committee the fact that this is the second time in a single session of a Canadian parliament that we are being asked to deal with a bill that contains within it a clause providing for compulsory arbitration on matters arising from a dispute between labour and management. I for one feel that if this is going to become a common occurrence in this chamber it is a subject matter that should give us cause for some serious thought before we repeat the performance for a second time in the same session.
In this connection I should like to draw to the attention of the committee the fact that the bill we now have before us is numbered Bill No. C-230, and that it was only recently, as far back as Bill No. C-215, that we were dealing with the subject matter of compulsory arbitration, shortly before the house entered into a period of recess. I find that launching upon this course of action in the Canadian parliament is something which to me is most repugnant. In my view this parliament and its members should be devoting attention to devising ways and means of avoiding entering into a proposal such as that contained in this clause.
I have not had the long and detailed experience on railway matters of some of my
September 1, 1966

colleagues in this party who have been participating in this debate, but I do feel that this particular clause in its implications goes far beyond this dispute. I feel that the members of the government who currently sit on the treasury benches, like those who have preceded them, when they were dealing with somewhat similar situations in the past, have not properly wrestled with the possible alternatives in presenting to parliament a particular course of action to bring this dispute to a conclusion.
Reference has already been made to the history of the major railway disputes in Canada, dating from 1950 to 1958 and 1960. I have to admit that I was not a member of this chamber prior to this occasion when parliament was wrestling with the question of bringing back into operation the national railway system. I had not arrived here in 1950, and as it happened I was temporarily absent in 1958 and 1960, the other previous occasions which have been mentioned in the debate.
However, I think that others who have preceded me in the discussion of this bill have made it abundantly clear that on each of those occasions parliament was asked to deal with a shotgun type of legislation to terminate a railway strike in this country. I well recall that when the Prime Minister opened the debate on this particular bill he waxed eloquent at considerable length upon his faith and belief in the principles of free collective bargaining; and in the next breath he said that he was going to bring the process of collective bargaining to an immediate termination, as far as it was possible for him to do so, in view of what I am sure he anticipated might be some resistance in this chamber.
I am not being particularly critical in any way of the present Prime Minister as contrasted with the position taken by his predecessors in that office who were faced with a parallel situation. What I am trying to say, Mr. Chairman, is that in view of this sequence of events in dealing with railway strikes, and in view of the fact that this has now reached the point that parliament has been asked to deal with disputes other than railway strikes, we should really begin to ask ourselves where we are going and what other alternative there is to this proposal that is now before us.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
I would remind the Prime Minister and the committee that a bill is in the parliamentary hopper at the present time designed to give
7983
Legislation Respecting Railway Matters the public service the right of collective bargaining. This is a measure which I am prepared to support. On the other hand, I see very little value in our going through the motions of giving collective bargaining rights to people in the public service if we know in our hearts that immediately they begin to exercise those rights in the normal way we shall be asked by the government of the day to yank those rights away from them. It is most illogical and nonsensical.
I referred earlier to Bill No. C-215. As the Prime Minister knows, when this matter was before us the members of my party tried to bring forward an alternative method of dealing with that situation. We suggested that the operating companies should be placed under a public trusteeship if it was our intention to ask those particular employees to return to work. We felt this was a technique of placing the two parties to the dispute in a position of balance. On the one hand, we were saying to the men involved that they should relinquish their rights to withold their services. On the other hand, we were saying to the employers: As long as this dispute continues you will not have the right to operate this concern.
We proposed that there should be open-ended mediation, with a terminal date in the bill representing what we thought was a reasonable period of time to allow the two parties to arrive at a solution of their problems, bearing in mind public opinion in the country. This, we felt, was at least one alternative to the shotgun tactics which we are being asked to approve in this bill as we were asked earlier by the government to agree to in Bill No. C-215. I have heard the Minister of Labour as well as the Prime Minister talk about free collective bargaining and their desire to see it function. I must say that I was surprised, indeed I was hurt, by the hasty and somewhat angry rejection on the part of the government of the proposal we put forward in all sincerity and good faith in the hope that it might be helpful, indicating that if it were acceptable to the government a fair majority of members were prepared to deal with this matter in a way which did not require the forcing of a solution through compulsory arbitration.
However, that matter is not before the committee at this moment. I am not even certain that this would be the most appropriate way of approaching the problems raised by a national rail strike. Two major railway lines are involved, one publicly owned and the other privately owned. I freely admit that in my own view the whole situation would be
September 1, 1966
7984	COMMONS
Legislation Respecting Railway Matters a lot simpler if we had one integrated railway system and public ownership. However, we are dealing with the situation which now exists and it seems to me that another possible way in which this matter could be settled would be to remove clause 10 entirely from the bill and substitute some provision for what I would again call open-ended mediation and negotiation with a proviso that if the parties had not been able to resolve their disagreements by a certain date the question would be returned to parliament. In the light of the evidence adduced during the mediation proceedings and the positions taken by the parties, parliament could then make a further determination of the issue on the basis of the facts as then known, including the extent to which the parties had been prepared to bargain in good faith and so on.
This would appeal to me as being another possible alternative worthy of consideration in a situation such as that created by a national rail strike. There may be yet another alternative which would make this bill more acceptable to those of us who have at heart the right of citizens to engage in free collective bargaining but who are yet prepared to recognize that there are situations where in the national interest it is not possible to allow a particular group of workers to withdraw their services. Instead of including in the bill provision for compulsory arbitration with a binding determination to be made, there could be a clause containing some form of provision or suggestion, or indeed an order from this parliament, to the effect that the parties might find it a course of wisdom to agree between themselves on some form of arbitration on one or more of the issues to be received between them.
I realize I cannot move that this clause be abolished. An attempt has been made to amend it. I shall not attempt to amend it in the terms I have suggested. I recognize that the government has embarked on the course of action proposed in this bill. I recognize too that the situation which faces this country is a serious one and that some action by parliament is required without too much delay. Unless the governement is prepared to indicate of its own initiative that it is willing to give consideration to some alternative to the terms of clause 10, then all I can do is to say that when this question comes to a vote I intend to indicate my disagreement by voting in such a way as to indicate that I wish it was not there.


[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
I said previously that I do not pretend to have all the answers to the question. Because of the increasingly complex society in which we are living, the plain fact that more and more groups or elements in the fabric of our society are deciding to withdraw their services means that the impact upon us is all the greater. I say that we in this parliament should come to grips with the problem and arrive at an answer consistent with the ocn-cept of free men being able to live in a free society.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to make a few brief comments on compulsory arbitration. I am a member of a local of the International Association of Fire Fighters which has voluntarily given up the right to strike and acquiesced in compulsory arbitration. In their case this has worked well, but they are a different kettle of fish from railroaders.
One of the things I find most abhorrent about the speeches made by many hon. members on this bill is that they are completely closing their eyes to what they are saying and doing. We have seen the Prime Minister and others stand up and proclaim they are determined to maintain the rights of the railroaders, rights similar to those of other workers. From this I would assume that the railroaders have the right to withdraw their services, in other words, the right to strike. But though these hon. members say to the railroaders that they have the right to strike, at the same time they say to them that they do not have the right to stay on strike.
How ridiculous can we get? We say that we will maintain their right to strike but if the strike becomes effective and pressure is brought to bear we will take away that right. If we are going to take away that right, then what is the point of giving it to them in the first place? What kind of sham are we carrying on? If this is what the law of the land is going to be, then it is high time the railroaders realized it and found something else to take the place of these rights so freely given and so quickly taken away.

Mr. Chairman, I have a few observations to make but I shall borrow no more than ten minutes of the committee's time to deal with clause 11 and an amendment which I propose to move that I believe will cope effectively with the root issue of the whole problem before us. During discussion of clause 10 we heard something about collective bargaining procedures and compulsory arbitration and my amendment will, in another sense, deal with these problems.
Without in any way detracting from the tremendously valuable service which collective bargaining has performed in the past and recognizing that it is desirable to continue to pursue it as far as possible, nonetheless I do not accept the proposition that this method is inviolable in any and all conditions. Our complex and fast-moving modern industrial society, composed of groups of people becoming more and more identifiable and interrelated, must have available some additional means, when necessary, of dealing with settlements in wage disputes.
For reasons which I shall give later I am convinced while we can give great priority to the continued use of collective bargaining procedures, yet there will be from time to time sets of circumstances which demand new and different approaches to be taken, either alone or in conjunction with the collective bargaining procedures. I think that has been pretty well recognized during the course of the debate.
Right now we are in a transitional phase. The process of collective bargaining has attained great aims for labour and has been a useful adjunct for society. If not replaced it must be used along with other methods, and the same is true of compulsory arbitration. We as a society have learned to accept, sometimes cheerfully but mostly grudgingly,

On a co-operative basis, having the objective of securing the greatest good for the greatest number, we have reluctantly imposed upon ourselves a great many forms of compulsion, some of a negative kind and some which compel us to do certain things. There are many more we shall have to consider in the future, and so I must come to the proposition that the exigencies of our society may be such as to require people to accept imposed decisions. When it is clear and evident that the overriding requirement of society calls for it, this will have to be accepted by labour unions as well as by others. True enough, Mr. Chairman, a tremendously heavy burden falls on those who assert this proposition. It is a very heavy burden, and I suggest it is not a burden which can be discharged as the government is attempting to discharge it in this committee.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
Having reached this conclusion, I must therefore say I have not opposed this bill because it does contain provisions for imposing decisions and for overriding the collective bargaining process, if this should become essential. But there is another reason. I am not going to take the time to deal with it in detail. However, there is a very interesting article by the famous historian Arthur Toynbee which appeared a short time ago and which sets forth that certain segments of society, particularly industry, capital, land owners and powerful labour unions, now have the power, the strength and the opportunity to assert such pressures that from time to time the share of the national wealth which they take is larger than that which on an equitable basis should be theirs in relation to those who have not this power to exert pressure.
There are millions of people in this country, pensioners, older people, salaried people, who are not organized, as well as small farmers who are dependent upon export markets, who have not the pressure, force or organization to exert any undue influence on their own behalf. Consequently the forces of particularly powerful groups in certain segments of society are able to pry out of the national wealth more than their fair share. I have no hesitation in saying this applies equally to certain segments of industry as it does to some labour unions.

When the government accepts, as it must accept, its responsibility and in an extraordinary set of circumstances brings us here, as it has now, and asks parliament to pass legislation of this kind, leaving the final decision to third parties outside of parliament, I suggest with great deference it is not discharging its full duty. It is incumbent upon the government, and I suggest it probably is incumbent upon parliament, to see the matter through to its ultimate conclusion.
I suggest that the whole debate has indicated the correctness of what I say. Most of the speeches and many of the amendments have been directed toward placing within the four corners of this legislation various measures which hon. members honestly and legitimately feel should be part of the final agreement, the final arrangement under which, after the workers have gone back and the strike is over, a solution finally will be reached. I suggest, therefore, that clause 11 as it now stands falls short of a discharge on the part of the government of the responsibility which it should have.
In clause 11 the bill provides that a regulation appointing a board of arbitrators shall be laid before the House of Commons not later than five days after the day the regulation is made. It then is a subject for debate and the house, of course, has the privilege of setting it aside. This accepts in part my view. I suggest in the first instance that this process should be reversed. I suggest that the regulation should be laid before the house and not become law until accepted by the house. I suggest further that any decision of the board of arbitrators, when and if it is essential-I hope it may not be-should also be laid before the House of Commons and should not become effective until it is passed by the house.
My very strong submission, Mr. Chairman, is that the unique, extraordinary combination of facts and circumstances which has brought us here and has led to the introduction of this measure will continue until the final settlement is made and that this house, and particularly the government, must accept this responsibility and must ensure, for the protection in the first instance of the workers, that the final results which are achieved are fair, equitable and reasonable and, second, must ensure that the result which finally is reached by the arbitrators is one which in its relation to society as a whole is also a proper and fair one. I am sure, Mr. Chairman, that

Every speech which 1 heard indicated the views of members of this house who honestly and seriously are concerned. Clause 10 sets out the powers and terms of reference for the arbitrators and surely that is enough without the whole matter being brought back to parliament. That would be unnecessary and illogical.
Mr. Chairman, I had intended to speak again, but having heard the persuasive words of the hon. member for York South I should like to say only that I accept his arguments.

Mr. Chairman, I have listened with a great deal of interest to this debate and at this time I should like to make reference to the amendment now before us. He said: Mr. Speaker, on September 14, 1964 I rose in the last parliament on the resolution stage preceding a bill which might now be called, I suppose, the precursor of the bill on which I am now speaking. I persuaded the committee to say that the introduction of the bill was expedient, and that is really, sir, where the expediency ended. In order to get any further consideration of the bill in that session I had to persuade my not altogether unwilling colleague, the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Mcllraith), to strangle the child in the cradle and to send the remains to a parliamentary committee where it was dissected for several weeks by all sorts of interested parties.
I have done a little better this time, sir. I got this bill through the committee stage without making a speech, and if any member of the house feels he was deprived in any way because I was not able to do that, notwithstanding the layman's guide to the bill which was circulated the other day, I would commend to him-and it is not always that I look at my previous utterances with the same approval as I do this one-the speech I made on September 14, 1964, because I think that nearly every opinion I expressed in it is thoroughly justified.
There is only one about which I feel a little shamefaced. I said at the beginning that it has been suggested to me that I was introducing a revolutionary measure. Well, sir, that was certainly one revolution that failed, and after the experiences in this house this week, at this hour, at which it is hard even for an enthusiast like me not to regard this bill as rather an anticlimax, it is a little hard, in the shopworn state in which I find myself tonight, to feel much like a revolutionary.

Perhaps if we can achieve something between the speed of revolutions and the speed of glaciers we might hope to make some progress with this measure.
In retrospect I do not think it would have been possible in 1964, even if there had been parliamentary time and even if that bill had seemed to that parliament as important as I like to think it was, to have passed this bill through parliament even if we had had the necessary priorities. Moreover, I think it is a good thing it was not passed. I have read all the editorials that anybody has clipped for me in all the great metropolitan newspapers, and in some of the others, about how this terrible crisis came upon us because we in this parliament were collectively so negligent since 1961 that we have done nothing about this railway problem.

I had also the inestimable advantage of reading the editorial in the Globe and Mail. It is a wonderful thing for politicians that they have this public conscience every morning to remind them of their deficiencies. The editorial
September 1, 1966

is entitled, "Can politics be kept out of transportation?"
Well, sir, there is only one place in Canada where anybody could be so far divorced from the realities of Canadian life that he could possibly write an editorial with that title, and that is in the city of Toronto, and perhaps even there only in the editorial offices of the Globe and Mail. Anybody who knows anything about the history of this country knows that there would have been no Canadian polity without transportation, and without a polity there would have been no politics. I said this once before in the house but I think it is worth repeating: Transportation has the capacity to arouse emotions and prejudices and to obscure the vision of most people even more completely than questions of race, religion or language.
It is right that it should be so. It is essential that it should be so, because without adequate transportation, there never would have been the kind of Canada we have; without the maintenance of effective transportation we never could have a united, efficient or agreeable country. This is what I understand by politics in transportation and I make no apology for it. On the day we cease to have politics in transportation, we will cease to have a free country.
Having said that, sir, I have to admit for the benefit of my colleagues on my right the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) and the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer), that there is a little germ of truth in what came out of Toronto this morning. There are two kinds of politics that we could have in transportation. One is the kind of politics which up to now I have been referring to; the kind of politics which means that in our collective wisdom, plus a certain amount of distributive foolishness, we do try in this house, despite partisan considerations, to get some kind of consensus of what will be suitable to bind this country together from Bonavista to Vancouver Island.

speechtext:
I would have to ask the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer) whether he knew the words to sing it. But I do not think my speech needs that kind of illustration.
There is another kind of politics which undoubtedly the editorial writer had in the back of his mind, and that is the kind of politics which, no matter which place we represent-even a place so self-sufficient as Toronto that it needs no transport-tempts all of us to see the selfish interests of individuals, groups or sometimes even of regions above the broader interests of the whole community.
That kind of partisanship and that kind of politics I quite agree we must try to keep out of our consideration of this measure if collectively we are to achieve something really

Transportation
useful for the country. I do hope that in the light of the circumstances in which we now find ourselves, while all of us will keep fully in mind the necessity for seeing that the point of view of every part of this country is adequately represented and fairly treated in a transportation policy, we will not push these regional and local interests to the point where it is difficult to reach a consensus of view that does meet the real national interest.
I know that there are in the house broadly two ideological views about transportation, and particularly about railways. Though this measure that I am introducing tonight is not by any means exclusively concerned with railways, it is mainly concerned with railways apart from the first part of the bill.
If I may once again allude to something which was said in an earlier debate today, I think by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett), it was very clearly stated that there were those who felt that a public monopoly of the railways would be preferable, more efficient and would remove a lot of problems which exist because of the fact that we have two main railways, and a certain number of other local railways in the country at the present time.
That view is one which I think is quite
tenable. There are a lot of arguments which could be made in its favour. But there are also a great many arguments on the other side. As I indicated two years ago-my views on this have not changed, and here there is cabinet solidarity because the views of the government have not changed-our view is that we do not think that on balance it would be an advantage at the present time to have only one railway in this country. We think that at the present time it is, on balance, better to make do with the basic situation which we have. We think that the rather limited amount of competition which exists at the present time-I would be the first to admit it is very limited, and I think too limited-between the railways themselves as well as between the railways and other forms of transportation serves the country better than would the other system.
However, Mr. Speaker, this is not the subject matter of the debate. Is is true that hon. members who wish to do so can assail this legislation and say that we should just scrap the whole system and have a different one. What we are seeking to do here-and perhaps this is why I was a little extravagant in the language I used two years ago when I said that what I proposed was revolutionary-is
[Mr. Pickersgill.l
not to scrap the basic corporate structure of the railways, or of any other form of transport at the present time, but to create a framework within which they can operate in a way which, in our view, will not only better serve the public-which is the main consideration-but which will also better insure the Canadian treasury and the Canadian taxpayers against unnecessary and undue charges, and in some cases duplicated charges for duplicated services, which do nothing except add to the costs which all of us both as a community and as individuals have to bear.
I think it is important to remind hon.
members, although they know it very well, that for nearly 80 years after confederation the railways were so much the most important mode of transportation in the country that they had in most areas a virtual monopoly in the carriage of goods, and pretty close to a monopoly in the carriage of people over any distance. That monopoly was mitigated in most areas of the country only by water transport, which of course is a much more ancient mode of transportation in Canada and was the original mode by which the country was opened up.
However, during this long period there existed the feeling which I think nearly always exists in any country where large and powerful bodies exercise an almost exclusive jurisdiction of any kind over things that enter into the lives and the livelihoods of nearly everybody, namely that this powerful force in the country had to be controlled by the public.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, this measure of control was established by the Laurier government in 1903, when the Board of Railway Commissioners was first established. From 1903 up to the present day, though there have been occasional changes in the ground rules, fundamentally we have continued to take the view that public regulation of the actions and charges of the railways is essential in the public interest.
This monopoly was mitigated in some respects, as I say, where there were obvious alternative sources of transport, such as the lakes area. It was more and more mitigated as modern highways were developed. The railway strike of 1950 transferred a lot of goods to other forms of transportation, particularly road transportation; and gradually in many parts of the country, with the development of air traffic, in respect to many forms of commodity, and above all in the
September 1, 1966

transport of human beings, that monopoly
has been eroded and in large part has disappeared.
It is not often that I pay tribute to the right hon. gentleman who leads the opposition, and I am sorry he is not here this evening, but he did one very good thing when he appointed the MacPherson commission. That commission made what I regard as a first rate report. It has stood up well, even after four or five years of exposure to the public gaze. It is true that circumstances have changed that some of these specific recommendations to deal with specific problems are no longer wholly appropriate, because some of the problems have changed their aspect. But the basic approach of the report was a new one. It was that there has been a development of alternative and competitive modes of transport in most parts of the country for most classes of travel, and that the kind of regulation of railway charges and practices by a regulatory body which may have been needed in the past was no longer essential for the protection of the public.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
Habits die hard. It has been very hard to get through our heads the idea that this has become true, and if we do not make a real effort of imagination it will be hard to appreciate the fact that many regulations which in the past were necessary in the public interest have simply become shackles in the present.
This is one of the exercises we have to perform if we are to make any basic improvement in the situation of the Canadian railways, and in their capacity to serve the Canadian public without placing undue burdens on the treasury. It is also necessary to make sure that we do not burden the public with services which have ceased to be essential because other modes of transport have taken their place. I have said before in the house that in no country in the world with which effective comparisons can be made is there a greater cost imposed on the community per capita in respect of transport services than is the case in Canada. This is true in respect of any country about which I know anything. It may not be true of Russia, though I doubt whether the density of the population there in relation to its transport facilities is any less than it is in our own country.
To put it in another way, the cost of transport enters more largely into the cost of 23033-506
Transportation
living and the cost of doing business of virtually every Canadian, on the average, than it does into the costs borne by citizens in any comparable country. It also happens that there is no other large country which depends to the extent this country does upon external income for the livelihood of its people. There is no country the per capita income of whose people is derived to such a large extent from outside the country as is the case in Canada.
In order to maintain this income it is essential that we should be competitive in the world we live in. Our transport services must be as efficient and as economical as possible. I cannot stress either of these things too much. After a great deal of deliberation and a great deal of discussion with people far more expert than I can ever hope to be, I came to the conclusion some six or eight months ago that in one respect we should make a more fundamental approach to this whole problem of national transportation than was envisaged two years ago when the bill was introduced at that time.
Because of my experience with other modes and forms of transport, for which I have a responsibility in so far as there is a public responsibility, I have reached the conclusion that one of the most important things of all is to have one unified organ of government divorced from any of these different1 modes of transport which would look at all of them, compare one with another and, when considering the regulation of one, would take account of what was happening in the other fields and determine whether we were getting the best value by spending public money on railways, for example, or whether it would be better to scrap a branch of a railway and concentrate on a highway or an air line.
We ought to be doing a lot more of this in Canada than we are today, if we are not to be burdened with expensive services which will not support themselves and for which the users cannot pay-services which therefore become an increasing burden on the treasury.
I do not think anything illustrates this more clearly than what has happened in the seven years since 1959. In those seven years, on three occasions, however this may have been disguised, the greater part of the increased wage bill of the Canadian railways has been passed on to the taxpayers of Canada-$20 million in 1959, $50 million in 1961 and another $30 million in 1966. So we are now paying out of the treasury $100 million a year. It seems to me, and it seems

September 1, 1966
Transportation
to some of my colleagues, that this process cannot go on without grave danger to the Canadian economy and to the well-being of all Canadians.
I think we are better able to appreciate this danger which has been brought home to us this week, so that we may be better able to overcome local prejudices and local tastes for the old and for the familiar, even when they have ceased to perform a function commensurate with its cost. Of course, it is easy for me to recommend that redundant services in Ontario or British Columbia, the prairies, Quebec or possibly, even the maritime provinces, should be curtailed.

I know there are some people in the house as well as some outside the house who fear that this-I forget who first coined the original phrase-could be a bureaucratic monster. I hope it will not. That certainly is not the intention. The intention is precisely the opposite. The intention and desire of the government is to amalgamate the three existing organisms and to provide certain other services in an effort, if I dare use the word and if it is not going to do my cause any harm, at integration.
I recognize at once that we have not reached the stage of common uniforms, and therefore it is provided in the bill that there will be a series of committees dealing with specific aspects of transportation and performing most of the functions now performed by the existing agencies. There will be other committees to perform functions in relation to interprovincial and international highway traffic at such time as the government may decide that in the public interest the present arrangements for dealing with them can no longer be continued.
There are some difficulties there, and I hasten to repeat what I said the other day that there is no present and immediate intention of taking on this task without full consultation with the provincial governments, and the fullest co-ordination. It is a very difficult field. It is quite unlike the railways because the highways are owned by the crown in the right of the provinces and the degree and nature of the jurisdiction and regulations that it is possible for parliament effectively to exercise-whatever the theoretical position may be-is very limited.
There is another field in which there may not be very much to do for some time, and that is in the transportation of solids by pipe line. This is something we know is coming and it did seem desirable, when we were attempting to foresee as much as we could the various modes of transportation, to do something so that we would have the machinery to deal with this problem when it does become of some importance.
It will also be competent for the commission to establish other committees, either on a permanent or ad hoc basis, to deal with particular problems. But I think the main reason why I came to the conclusion, and the main reason I was able to convince my colleagues that this was good to recommend to

When hon. members stop to think how vital transport is to the country and how large a part it plays in our whole economy, it is little short of disgraceful to realize that when a minister wishes to employ an expert in almost any field of transport he has to go outside the country either to the United States or to the United Kingdom. It is not because we do not have good Canadians with expertise, but it is because they all are employed with interests of one kind or another which in some respects are different from the public interest. This means that when you get these experts, if it takes them six months to do the job, they take four months educating themselves at the expense of the Canadian public, one month carrying on their investigation and another month writing their reports.
There is an awful lot to be said for applying that education continuously, and for educating Canadians. I do not mean that we are going to have a whole host of experts in the commission, but I do believe that if we keep this matter under continuous review we may in some of our universities-and I may say that some initiative seems to have been taken in this field in my own university in Manitoba-find that we will get some people in Canada who can be employed, and in respect of whom we will have the assurance that they are not in any way tied to any existing interests. Because they will be people who know the environment in which they live, they will not have to spend half of the time in which they are employed finding out what is the problem.
I believe that this plan will work. I do not say that it will end forever the neeed for any more royal commissions on transportation, but it will vastly reduce the need for them. Most of these studies will be done much more efficiently and much more quickly by people who are really familiar with the background of the matter which they are studying.

There are other things; there are certain kinds of studies which the Minister of Transport or the government as a whole may wish to have done in order to be of assistance to them in making up their minds as to the kind of policies which are to be recommended. In cases of this nature I should think it would be very unwise to have these working studies made public, because if ministers are to be of any use and not just ciphers, they must be allowed to exercise their own judgment.
Apart altogether from any other aspects of the matter, if you have an expert study made and exercise your judgment upon it, and then the expert study is published, it puts both the minister and the expert in really quite an awkward position. I think it is quite contrary to our system of responsible government to do that. I know there are many distinguished authorities on transportation in Canada, like Mr. Douglas Fisher who was a former member of this house, who do not subscribe to this view and who think that everything should be done in the full glare of publicity. Maybe; it is a view. I think, however, that most people who have had experience in government, and not just experience in criticizing governments, would realize that this is not necessarily so. Well, it may have some advantages; and sometimes I think you need to shed a little light in some of these dark places, even in the Department of Transport. There are many occasions when you can have freedom of discussion, freedom to express opinions, and change opinions only if you do not have to expose your vanity.

Part V of the bill carries out, but in a rather different way from what was envisaged in the previous bill, the principle enunciated by the MacPherson commission, namely that those services which parliament requires the railways to perform in the national or social interest, but which are not remunerative, should have their losses largely paid for out of treasury. I refer to the uneconomic services, to use a loose term, which give the railways a reason for saying they are unable to pay adequate wages and so on. become as great as what is left of the transitional subsidies. The transitional grants will then disappear and the other subsidies take their place. In this way we will have plenty of time to do a proper costing. This will not be guesswork. In the meantime we will get rid of this huge, undifferentiated subsidy which is now being paid and which is a very unbusinesslike way, to put it mildly, of dealing with this problem.
In respect of rates other than the Crowsnest rates and the maritime freight rates, which of course will not be touched until the study is completed, and any new policy resulting from that study is evolved, apart from these rates and the Atlantic and eastern rates which are to be continued indefinitely, as well as the freight rate reduction in the Atlantic provinces which is to be continued for two more years, all other freight rates charged by the railways will fall into two classes. There will be those rates which are imposed upon captive shippers in cases where there are no alternative competitive ways of shipping goods. Those rates will be protected by a maximum rate and this will be the highest rate that the railway can charge. This does not mean that they will necessarily charge that rate, because most captive shippers today have agreed charges of one type or another. We have put two or three bills through this house in this session under which the railway branch lines have been based upon these agreed charges. However, every captive shipper will be protected by a maximum rate and the railway will not be able to charge a rate higher than that.
In the case of shippers who have an alternative mode of shipping which is genuinely competitive, the railways will be allowed to fix their charges, just as do other carriers such as trucks, ships or planes. In the main they will be able to compete for the traffic with other forms of transport. However, they will not be allowed to carry this competition to the point where the rates charged will become unremunerative. In other words, the railways will not be allowed to charge less than the cost of carrying the goods in order to put some competitor out of business. The rates they charge must be remunerative and the necessary provisions are contained in this bill to ascertain, in case of complaints, that they are. Those are the basic principles embodied in the railway section of the bill.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext: The question I have to ask is probably the most important that could be asked of the minister, because it has to do with the matter of financing and, in particular, in the way in which this commission he is appointing to handle transportation is going to obtain information about railway operations. The minister says there will be expert help, he hopes, employed by the board. What I had in mind particularly was to ask him if there will be a firm of competent accountants engaged who will give their services to this board so that we may not have to depend entirely upon the figures the railways may supply. We should like to have impartial estimates for the use of the board and, I hope, for the use of the parliamentary committee on transport. This is my first question.

It would be absolutely impossible for this proposed commission to do its work, I think, if it had to depend upon the accounting information provided by the railways, without any independent examination. Now, precisely how that would be done, whether it would be done by hiring outside experts or by engaging experts for the staff of the commission, it would be foolish of me to try to anticipate. I suspect both means would be used. I suspect they would have to have a considerable basic staff to do their costing. I would think that from time to time big problems would arise that were beyond

At the end of my remarks I had intended to make a pronosal which I thought would be helpful to the house in moving more swiftly to grapple with the major problems on second reading. We have eliminated the resolution stage which, under the old rule, used to give members a chance to ask questions and get some points cleared up. This particular bill has in it at least a score of major principles which I feel sure every member feels need clarification. The mere fact that when the minister spoke on second reading tonight many of us wanted to ask questions is indicative of the fact that we have to know a great deal more before we can vote on the principles of this bill at second reading.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
The proposal I want to make, which apparently we will be able to consider overnight, follows other precedents in the house. I want to move at the end of my remarks, which I presume will be tomorrow morning, that the subject matter of Bill No. C-231 be referred to the standing committee on transportation, provided however that despite this motion the said bill shall remain on the order paper

as an order for second reading without prejudice to the right to make or proceed with the motion for second reading.
What I am suggesting, Mr. Speaker, for the consideration of the party leaders or house leaders of the various parties is that before we can intelligently vote on the many principles which are inherent in this omnibus legislation we might be able to speed up things quite a bit if we were to move straight into committee stage, before continuing our full debate on the principle. I intend to make in the committee stage, if I am allowed, some proposals which I think can speed up the lengthy debate that I foresee on two sections of the bill. My proposals are five in number and are very simple, and I am sure that when they are heard will be recognized as a device to save a long, drawn out debate that we cannot otherwise avoid. I put this suggestion forward for the consideration of the house leaders and party leaders in the hope that this type of proposal, which is used mainly on private members motions and has only been used once on a government bill, will be considered in relation to this legislation.
In the few minutes that are left I want to make a remark or two about what the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) has said. He stated that the MacPherson report was a sound report, that it was a tremendous effort to get at the basic considerations of the fundamentals of the railway industry. I agree with that statement, but there is one thing wrong with it. That commission was set up in 1959 when, in the minds of most of the economists and business people of this country, the railways were looked upon as a declining and almost dying industry. However, since 1961 the revolution has occurred, and the revolution is that instead of 400 million bushels of grain moving in a crop year in western Canada we are now moving 800 million bushels.
The railways are a type of industry which is operated mostly on a fixed cost basis. If you increase the number of units moving in a fixed cost operation, you drastically reduce your costs. Today no one in his right mind would even suggest that there is any loss involved in the haulage of grain. There has never been any conclusive proof that there was ever any loss. Not even the railroaders would suggest, except in a clownish moment, that there was any loss on the haulage of grain.

What I am trying to say is that this bill today, in 1966, is much better than the bill produced in 1964, but it is still hanging on to that old shibboleth that the industry is a dying industry which we must surround and protect.
I suggest that what we should do is to face the fact that not only is grain going to be a large item, but that by 1970 there will be more tons of potash hauled over the railways of western Canada to the west coast alone than there is wheat now sent to the west coast. We have 12 new pulp and paper mills to build on the prairies over the next decade which must transport their products west or south. We also need to transport zinc, sulphur, molybdenum and coal, the production of which is increasing at a fantastic pace. So that instead of thinking that our railways are dead and dying, a precept to which this bill still clings to a certain degree, we should abolish this type of thinking and begin to take advantage of the fact that we now have the green light.
Fortunately, we have in this bill one clause that gives me hope. I think that in committee we can take a look at the facts and figures, the maps and so on, and can remove the great fear which exists in western Canada and has existed since the royal commission report was brought down, namely that 15, 20 or 25 per cent of the people will have their railway lines abandoned. That fear should be removed immediately.
This should be done not on a five year or ten year basis. They should be told right now that every application has gone out of the window and that not one application presently before the board will be considered. Then when you have done that, all of us in committee can sit down with the board, and I believe that within a few days we should begin to show the people of the three prairie provinces that this great fear which has been hanging over them has gone, that all we are going to consider is a direction to the railways to operate their systems efficiently.
The system operating in the west can be operated so efficiently that there will be no need for any subsidies whatever. We will make so much money for the railways in western Canada that perhaps they will begin to pay wages to their employees which equal those paid in other industries. We hope that we will be able to show so much profit for the railways in western Canada that instead of increasing freight rates, they will have to be reduced.

That is the philosophy which I express in my remarks, Mr. Speaker, and I apologize to all hon. members of the house for jumping right into the theme of my remarks without building up to them as I had intended. However, I do want to get this feeling of optimism rather than pessimism before the house.
On page after page of this bill are listed the gruesome details of the procedure for abandoning rail lines, how a poster must be put up at every station along the line warning the people that an application has been made to close it. Even though the board or the governor in council has decreed that a particular line shall not be abandoned for a certain time, the people are nevertheless served notice that it may be abandoned some day, perhaps five years from now, perhaps three years from now. It is like living on death row, with the certain knowledge that you are not going to be painlessly removed but are going to be strangled by a slow death.
This fear, as I say, has to be removed, and that is where parliament comes in. If we can go into committee and get a statement from the minister, then after we have explained what is in our minds I think that 90 per cent of this fear, which is held by the minister, will vanish.
I knew what the minister meant when he said that it is a question of balancing the local interest against the national interest. He also said that the old bill of 1964 was the precursor of this one. Let us leave off the "pre"; everybody curses that bill because they knew what it was. The first bill of 1964 was a farce, so far as rationalization was concerned, and it was a sell-out so far as costing was concerned. My hon. friend from Kindersley was right on the ball when he mentioned that in his question.
Tonight the minister said that he knew it would not be very easy to get this bill through the house, and he quietly appealed in a hopeless sort of way that we reduce the amount of fighting. I say that there is a positive way to get at this bill, and a positive way which will have the support of every westerner in this house.
We are the lifeblood of the railways. We are also the biggest source of revenue that the railways have. We will make even more money for the railways. All we ask in exchange is that we take this rationalization concept and put it into effect. Then not in 10, 15 or 20 years-because that is what it will take when we get through all these ramifications-but in one, two or three years and

before 1970 we will be out of the subsidy business in western Canada and will have the peace of mind which we have not had for many a decade.
We know that there are one or two little joining up lines which have to be closed, and we do not oppose this; we welcome it. We know that we have tried for years to get the railway to abandon lines in certain places. Certain lines run parallel, and you can take out a fishing pole and touch them for mile after mile.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
This is hard to understand. We have known ever since the Duff report of 1934 that this was a losing situation for both railways. We note that the concept of joint running routes has been accepted. I can recall one case in Saskatchewan where the C.N.R. hauled grain 109 miles north and 100 miles south so that they would not have to cross a C.P.R. bridge. That is how archaic the system is. The C.P.R. was established on a favourable commercial basis but the C.N.R. was a hodge-podge and we have been paying the shot ever since. Now is the time to straighten out this hodge-podge and, without interfering with the right of the railways to manage their own affairs, say to them: For God's sake run the railways efficiently. If they will not do it, I want to see in this bill the power to require them to do it.
Maybe this is the principle which the government has in mind. I do not know what to recommend to my party. Should we support these principles when I do not know where the power lies? I should like the chance to question the minister before I vote on this bill on second reading.
I am sure the minister will find me as helpful as I was in the past on those committees which he mentioned tonight. After bill C-120 had been introduced at the resolution stage, he spoke and I spoke. I said I would support the principles which I thought were contained in the bill. The former member for Port Arthur was not as gullible as I was. He was suspicious. But I believed the government would not neglect the opportunity to place these railways on a national basis.

Thank you for your protection, Mr. Speaker. 1 think you understand the difficulties under which I am working. I understand precisely why the minister has raised this question and it demonstrates, in my opinion, that the suggestion I have made is a sensible one. If these fears could be removed the minister might be amazed how forward looking we can be. If the minister would back this proposal and use his good offices with hon. members in all parts of the house, because there must be unanimous agreement, I think we would have a really good session because our ideas have advanced considerably during these past few years.
I wish to turn now, to another matter, one which is, I believe, the guts of the railway bill. This is where the big quarrel will take place. We shall fight on the question of maximum rate controls.
