If the minister wishes to put it like that, I will accept it. I will add something else-that none of us in this house is competent, either. When the question of the Crowsnest pass rates came up there were protests from all western provinces. The C.P.R. hired one of the most able and competent cost accountant firms they could find in the United States, who had done cost accounting on railways, to look at the figures for 1958 for the carriage of grain in Canada. After several months work they came up with figures allocating certain costs, and said that on the carriage of grain in 1958 the C.P.R. had lost $17 million.
This caused an uproar from the three prairie provinces and they decided to spend good money on a similar study. They went out and hired an equally able, experienced cost accounting firm in the United States to examine exactly the same figures as the previous firm had done. This second firm allocated them slightly differently and said no, the C.P.R. did not lose money that year, but had made $2 million. What was the royal commission to do? It went out and got another firm of equally able, competent people to examine the figures and they said, "Neither is right; we think it is probably in between," and so they set the loss at $500,000. This is a humorous anecdote of what actually happened. The Board of Transport Commissioners are simply not in this costing league. This is not new. The gas industry has been operating in North America for 60 years and still no costing system has been decided upon.
When the experts cannot agree, then we in parliament have some part to play. We shall have to lay down the terms of reference between these experts and say that for the next two years or five years this shall be the costing system, and perhaps change it at the end of that period to a new system.

Now, Mr. Speaker, I have gone beyond ten o'clock because I wanted to get something on the record tonight in answer to what the minister had said, first to make absolutely clear that I think we in this house should reject this pessimistic feeling about railroads.
Railways have been and will continue to be a very important part of our transportation system. Over and over again the railways have demonstrated that when you kick them high enough they can do fantastic things. This year, after we in the House of Commons finally blew our top, what the railways were able to do with the movement of grain was unbelievable. They actually brought in more motive power. They railroaded as never before. One of these days they are going to get so smart that they are going to build or buy a proper car for carrying grain which, instead of taking 20 minutes to load, can be loaded or unloaded in 12, 14 or 16 seconds. Then they will find their cost-profit relationship sweet.
Therefore I say that in this matter of looking at the railway bill we have to examine it minutely and realize we are setting the basic framework on which railways will operate, and which may guide the transportation industry of this country for a generation or two.
The question of the super board is one on which many of our members will want to ask the minister many questions. We want to know how it is going to relate the functions of a railway, in the traditional sense, to a railway looking on itself as an arm of the transportation industry. There is not a railway company in existence that should not be a full transportation company. If they can transport things by rail they should also be in the air business, the water business, the hovercraft business and the pipe line business, in fact in any other thing that transports goods, and that should be an integral part of their operations in order to achieve maximum efficiency.
Here in Canada where so many of our goods will be carried by pipe lines, the railways are naturals to go into the business of operating and building pipe lines, in some cases in competition with each other, and in other cases working jointly. This is one of the things we should see popping up in this bill.
But as I read the bill all the enthusiasm for what a railway company can become in Canada, with these great distances which are a great opportunity for them, dies as I look at the duties of this super board. What are their

duties? They are to study this, study that, study this, and after a while study this. We need the statistics, yes; but surely parliament can give them some direction as to what we want them to do. There is another series of questions. If we take over the interprovincial trucking lines and the interprovincial buses and reach the point where the railways carry passengers on rail while the other carries passengers on rubber, and where the one carries freight on rail and the other carries freight on rubber, what is the relationship to the rate setting pattern? The railways are prohibited from setting a rate below compensatory levels. What is the situation in respect of the trucks. This is the sort of question to which the government will have to have answers. We have to have those answers before we know how to vote on the principles.
